> ## [doc:https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-09-05-anatomy-of-vllm] (doc) Inside vLLM: Anatomy of a High-Throughput LLM Inference System
> # Inside vLLM: Anatomy of a High-Throughput LLM Inference System
> ### From paged attention, continuous batching, prefix caching, specdec, etc. to multi-GPU, multi-node dynamic serving at scale
> 1. LLM engine & engine core: fundamentals of vLLM (scheduling, paged attention, continuous batching, etc.)
> 2. Advanced features: chunked prefill, prefix caching, guided & speculative decoding, disaggregated P/D
> 4. Serving layer: distributed / concurrent web scaffolding
> 5. Benchmarks and auto-tuning: measuring latency and throughput

> ## LLM Engine & Engine Core
> ### Scheduler
> That will go into more detail behind prefill/decode perf profiles.
>
> The scheduler prioritizes decode requests — i.e. those already in the running queue.
>
> 1. Computes number of blocks — determines how many new KV-cache blocks (n) must be allocated. Each block stores 16 tokens by default. For example, if a prefill request has 17 new tokens, we need ceil(17/16) = 2 blocks.
>
> ## Advanced Features — extending the core engine logic
> 1. Chunked prefill
> 2. Prefix caching
> 4. Speculative decoding
> 5. Disaggregated P/D (prefill/decoding)
>
> ### Chunked prefill
> Chunked prefill is a technique for handling long prompts by splitting their prefill step into smaller chunks. Without it, we could end up with a single very long request monopolizing one engine step disallowing other prefill requests to run. That would postpone all other requests and increase their latency.
>
> For example, let each chunk contain n (=8) tokens, labeled with lowercase letters separated by "-". Executing the full prefill for P would then take ≥ 3 engine steps (> can happen if it's not scheduled for execution in one of the steps), and only in the last chunked prefill step would we sample one new token.
>
> Here is that same example visually:
>
> Implementation is straightforward: cap the number of new tokens per step. If the requested number exceeds long_prefill_token_threshold, reset it to exactly that value.
>
> In vLLM V1, you enable chunked prefill by setting long_prefill_token_threshold to a positive integer. (Technically, it can happen irrespective of this, if the prompt length exceeds the token budget we truncate it and run a chunked prefill.)
>
> ### Prefix Caching
> To explain how prefix caching works, let's take the original code example and tweak it a bit:
>
> Prefix caching avoids recomputing tokens that multiple prompts share at the beginning - hence prefix.
>
> The crucial piece is the long_prefix: it's defined as any prefix longer than a KV-cache block (16 tokens by default).

> ## Features

> ### Advanced Scheduling

> - **Prefix Caching**: Share KV cache blocks for common prefixes

> - **Speculative Decoding**: Use a draft model to speed up generation

> ## Key Concepts Explained
> ### PagedAttention
> Traditional inference pre-allocates KV cache for maximum sequence length, wasting memory:

> ### Continuous Batching
> Unlike static batching that waits for all sequences to finish:
>
> ### KV Cache
> Without caching, attention recomputes K,V for all tokens every step (O(n²)). With caching, we only compute K,V for new tokens (O(n)):

> ## [doc:https://zeroentropy.dev/concepts/vllm-serving/] (doc) vLLM Serving
> # vLLM Serving
> Its core innovations — PagedAttention for KV-cache memory management, continuous batching for throughput, and prefix caching for prompt reuse.
>
> - PagedAttention: KV cache as virtual memory
> - Continuous batching: don’t wait for slow sequences
> - Prefix caching: reuse the system prompt
>
> (2023, “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention”), vLLM stacks three core ideas — PagedAttention for KV-cache memory, continuous batching for compute, and prefix caching for prompt reuse — into a single serving engine that handles 2-10x more throughput than naive HuggingFace `generate()` on the same hardware (up to 24x on the original paper high-concurrency benchmarks).
>
> VLLM SERVING STACKPages, in flight, and shared.PAGED ATTENTION16 TOKENS / BLOCK · MEM UTIL ≈ 96%req 1req 2sharedone physical copysystem-prompt KV reused across requestssp1sp2u1u2CONTINUOUS BATCHINGGPU UTIL ≈ 90%slot 0slot 1slot 2slot 3ABCDEA done — E slots innaive1× tokens / secvLLM2–10× tokens / secpaged memory+continuous batching+prefix cache
>
> ## Why naive serving fails
> A transformer’s KV cache grows linearly with sequence length.
>
> ## Continuous batching: don’t wait for slow sequences
> Continuous batching is the second pillar. A batch of 32 with one slow sequence wastes 31 slots for the duration.
>
> Continuous batching swaps in new requests at every token step.
>
> ## Prefix caching: reuse the system prompt
> If 1000 requests share the same 4K-token system prompt, naive serving recomputes the prefix’s KV 1000 times. vLLM’s prefix caching uses PagedAttention’s block-sharing to compute the prefix once and reuse it across all requests sharing it.
>
> In practice this is a 30-90% latency reduction on the first token (TTFT) for high-concurrency workloads with shared prompts — agent workloads, RAG with templated system messages, structured-output pipelines. See caching strategies for the broader cache hierarchy.
>
> ## When vLLM is the wrong choice
> Secondary gotchas: prefix caching only helps if prefixes actually repeat (random prompts kill it), quantization can degrade quality on math-heavy or long-tail tasks, and multi-LoRA serving has per-adapter overhead at high QPS.
>
> ## Operational shape
> Memory KPI is KV-cache utilization (target ~90%+).
>
> ## [doc:https://zeroentropy.dev/concepts/continuous-batching/] (doc) Continuous Batching
> # Continuous Batching
> TL;DR
>
> The vLLM-style scheduling trick where requests join and leave a batch in-flight, dynamically.
>
> Author
>
> Alexander RochaFounding Engineer
>
> Continuous batching is the scheduling discipline behind every modern LLM serving stack — vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang. It increases throughput 5-20× over static batching by letting requests join and leave the in-flight batch every decode step.
>
> **The unit of scheduling is one token, not one request.** That single shift is what unlocked production-scale LLM serving.
>
> ## What continuous batching does
> The scheduler operates at _token-level_ granularity instead of request-level:
>
> 1. **Each step generates one token across the active batch.** Standard transformer decode.
> 2. **After each step, the scheduler:**
>    - Recomputes KV cache memory budget.
>
> ## Why it required PagedAttention
> Naive batching pre-allocates KV cache contiguous blocks per slot, sized for max generation length.
>
> vLLM’s PagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023) treats the KV cache like virtual memory — request KV is split into fixed-size pages, allocated on demand, can be non-contiguous.
>
> ## Where the technique matters for retrieval
> What's the difference between prefill and decode in a batched scheduler?
>
> **Prefill** processes the entire input prompt in one parallel pass — compute-bound, fast per-token, builds the initial KV cache. **Decode** generates output one token at a time — memory-bound, much slower per-token, appends to the KV cache.
>
> Continuous batching has to schedule both. Real schedulers chunk prefill into the same step as decode — vLLM’s “chunked prefill” splits a long prompt into pieces and interleaves prefill chunks with decode of other requests in the batch.
>
> The result is a single fused step that mixes a few decoding requests with a slice of one prefilling request.
>
> How does continuous batching interact with prompt-prefix caching?
>
> Prefix caching stores the KV pages for repeated prompt prefixes — a long system prompt shared across requests, a few-shot template, an agent’s stable instruction block. A request hitting the cache skips prefill on those tokens entirely; the scheduler attaches the cached pages and starts decode immediately.
>
> The prefill phase is the expensive one for long prompts; cache-hit requests skip it and slot into decode-only batches with millisecond latency. The throughput math improves dramatically — for an agent loop with a 10K-token system prompt and 200-token completions, prefix caching turns each call into a tiny decode-only step, and the batch can hold many more concurrent requests in the same VRAM budget.

> ## [doc:https://github.com/wanshuiyin/auto-claude-code-research-in-sleep/blob/15c0b799e6cd5fbc4da381a5786dd0bc2cdf15ee/docs/tutorials/kv_cache_speculative_decoding_tutorial.md] (doc) kv cache speculative decoding tutorial
> ### 3.2　Chunked Prefill（Sarathi-Serve）
>
> > 💡 **关键洞察** — prompt 越长，prefill 一次 forward 把 GPU 算力全占住，**正在 decode 的请求会被卡住**（head-of-line blocking）。
>
> Sarathi-Serve（Agrawal et al., OSDI 2024）把长 prefill 切成等大小 chunk，每个 iteration 调度一个 prefill chunk + 一批 decode token 一起跑：
>
> ```
>        传统：prompt 4096 → 一次 prefill 占满 GPU → decode 卡 100+ ms
>        Sarathi: prompt 切 4 个 chunk × 1024 → 每 iteration 跟 decode coalesce
> ```
>
> **Stall-free schedule**：保证每个 iteration 有 decode + prefill chunk 混跑，decode latency 抖动消失。论文实测 Mistral-7B 单 A100 服务能力相比 vLLM 提升 2.6×，Yi-34B 在 2×A100 上 3.7×。
>
> ### 3.3　Continuous Batching（Orca）
>
> 传统 static batching：等整个 batch 都跑完才放新请求进来——**短请求被长请求拖死**。Orca（Yu et al., OSDI 2022）把调度粒度从 request 改成 **iteration**：每次 forward 都检查一遍 batch 里有没有完成的（EOS），完成的踢出去、空位让新请求进来。
>
> > ✅ **vLLM = Orca 的 continuous batching + PagedAttention 内存管理** — 这两条加在一起把 LLM serving 吞吐拉到了之前的 24× 左右。
>
> ### 3.4　Prefix Caching
>
> 如果多个请求共享 prompt 前缀（如 system prompt、few-shot prompt），完全可以**复用同一份 KV cache**：
>
> - vLLM 的 prefix caching：用 hash(prompt prefix) 索引 cache page，命中则跳过 prefill
> - ChatGPT 这种 prompt-heavy 服务，prefix cache hit rate 可达 90%+，大幅减 prefill 开销
> - 实现关键：page-level 共享 + COW（copy-on-write），分支的请求只对自己的 page 写
>
> ## §4 KV Cache 优化路线
>
> ### 4.1　路线总览
>
> | 路线 | 核心 idea | 减少了什么 | 代表 |
> | --- | --- | --- | --- |
> | **共享 head**（MQA/GQA） | 多个 Q head 共享一组 K/V | KV head 数 $H \to G$ 或 1 | LLaMA-2/3, Mistral, PaLM |
> | **低秩压缩**（MLA） | 投影到低维 latent，cache latent 而非 K/V | head 维度有效减小 $d_\text{head} \to d_c/H$ | DeepSeek-V2/V3 |
> | **量化**（KIVI/KVQuant） | 把 cache 元素 fp16 → int4/int2 | bytes per element | KIVI, KVQuant, FP8 KV |
> | **稀疏化 / eviction** | 只保留"重要"位置的 K/V | $L_\text{ctx}$ 有效缩短 | H2O, StreamingLLM, TriForce |
> | **内存管理**（PagedAttention） | 不减小总量，但消除碎片 | fragmentation overhead | vLLM |
>

>       "url": "https://github.com/wanshuiyin/auto-claude-code-research-in-sleep/blob/15c0b799e6cd5fbc4da381a5786dd0bc2cdf15ee/docs/tutorials/kv_cache_speculative_decoding_tutorial.md",
>       "title": "kv cache speculative decoding tutorial",
>       "passages": [
>         {
>           "text": "### 3.2　Chunked Prefill（Sarathi-Serve）\n\n> 💡 **关键洞察** — prompt 越长，prefill 一次 forward 把 GPU 算力全占住，**正在 decode 的请求会被卡住**（head-of-line blocking）。\n\nSarathi-Serve（Agrawal et al., OSDI 2024）把长 prefill 切成等大小 chunk，每个 iteration 调度一个 prefill chunk + 一批 decode token 一起跑：\n\n```\n       传统：prompt 4096 → 一次 prefill 占满 GPU → decode 卡 100+ ms\n       Sarathi: prompt 切 4 个 chunk × 1024 → 每 iteration 跟 decode coalesce\n```\n\n**Stall-free schedule**：保证每个 iteration 有 decode + prefill chunk 混跑，decode latency 抖动消失。论文实测 Mistral-7B 单 A100 服务能力相比 vLLM 提升 2.6×，Yi-34B 在 2×A100 上 3.7×。\n\n### 3.3　Continuous Batching（Orca）\n\n传统 static batching：等整个 batch 都跑完才放新请求进来——**短请求被长请求拖死**。Orca（Yu et al., OSDI 2022）把调度粒度从 request 改成 **iteration**：每次 forward 都检查一遍 batch 里有没有完成的（EOS），完成的踢出去、空位让新请求进来。\n\n> ✅ **vLLM = Orca 的 continuous batching + PagedAttention 内存管理** — 这两条加在一起把 LLM serving 吞吐拉到了之前的 24× 左右。\n\n### 3.4　Prefix Caching\n\n如果多个请求共享 prompt 前缀（如 system prompt、few-shot prompt），完全可以**复用同一份 KV cache**：\n\n- vLLM 的 prefix caching：用 hash(prompt prefix) 索引 cache page，命中则跳过 prefill\n- ChatGPT 这种 prompt-heavy 服务，prefix cache hit rate 可达 90%+，大幅减 prefill 开销\n- 实现关键：page-level 共享 + COW（copy-on-write），分支的请求只对自己的 page 写\n\n## §4 KV Cache 优化路线\n\n### 4.1　路线总览\n\n| 路线 | 核心 idea | 减少了什么 | 代表 |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| **共享 head**（MQA/GQA） | 多个 Q head 共享一组 K/V | KV head 数 $H \\to G$ 或 1 | LLaMA-2/3, Mistral, PaLM |\n| **低秩压缩**（MLA） | 投影到低维 latent，cache latent 而非 K/V | head 维度有效减小 $d_\\text{head} \\to d_c/H$ | DeepSeek-V2/V3 |\n| **量化**（KIVI/KVQuant） | 把 cache 元素 fp16 → int4/int2 | bytes per element | KIVI, KVQuant, FP8 KV |\n| **稀疏化 / eviction** | 只保留\"重要\"位置的 K/V | $L_\\text{ctx}$ 有效缩短 | H2O, StreamingLLM, TriForce |\n| **内存管理**（PagedAttention） | 不减小总量，但消除碎片 | fragmentation overhead | vLLM |"
>         }

> ## [doc:https://launchdarkly.com/blog/llm-inference-optimization/] (doc) LLM inference optimization: Tutorial & Best Practices
> # LLM inference optimization: Tutorial & Best Practices
> ## **Summary of key LLM inference optimization concepts**
> | Concept | Description |
> |-|-|
> | Model parallelization techniques | Pipeline parallelism, tensor parallelism, and sequence parallelism help increase the throughput of LLM inference |
> | Quantized models | Quantization reduces model weight precision and activations, reducing the memory footprint. |
> | Model serving optimizations | In-flight batching and speculative decoding are serving optimizations that can help reduce latency. |
> | Capturing LLM inference metrics | Metrics like time for the first token and output tokens per second help assess the latency of your LLM deployment. |
>
> ## **Understanding LLM Inference**
> During inference, LLMs take in an input sequence of tokens known as prompts to generate an output.
>
> They also help optimize inference within a single GPU through techniques like batching and speculative execution.
>
> ## **Techniques for LLM inference optimization**
> - Model parallelization
>
> ### **Model parallelization techniques for LLM inference optimization**
> #### **Tensor parallelism**
> Tensor parallelism splits the neural network horizontally into several blocks. Each block is served through an independent GPU. This approach is especially beneficial in attention mechanisms, since several strategies can be used to independently manage the attention score generation and execute it in parallel.
>
> Attention enhancements like multi-query attention and grouped query attention are good candidates for parallel execution.
>
> A logical overview of tensor parallelism
>
> Similarly to the previous example, vLLM provides a startup option called ‘--tensor-parallel-size’ to enable this functionality. You can read more about it here.
>
> #### **Sequence Parallelism**
> Tensor parallelism works only in the case of independently manageable blocks like attention.
>
> You can read more about it here.
>
> ## **Closing thoughts**
> One way to optimize LLM inference is to share the processing workload and memory workload among several GPUs using pipeline, tensor, and sequence parallelism.

> ## [doc:https://jarvislabs.ai/blog/vllm-sglang-trtllm-comparison] (doc) vllm sglang trtllm comparison
> ## SGLang
> But SGLang puts a lot of focus on runtime efficiency, prefix reuse, and structured generation.
>
> One of the most important ideas in SGLang is **RadixAttention**.
>
> Instead of recomputing the KV cache for the same prefix again and again, SGLang stores and reuses shared prefixes using a radix-tree-based cache.
>
> - RadixAttention for efficient prefix caching
> - Chunked prefill for better scheduling of long prompts
> - Speculative decoding support
> - Structured generation and constrained decoding support
>
> It also tries to optimize the full serving runtime around how requests are structured and how much computation can be reused.
>
> ## Difference Between vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM
> | Area | vLLM | SGLang | TensorRT-LLM |
> |-|-|-|-|
> | KV cache design | PagedAttention | RadixAttention and paged KV cache | Optimized KV cache management |
> | Prefix reuse | Prefix caching | Radix-tree-based prefix caching | Prefix caching support depends on runtime/config |
>
> ## Conclusion
> **SGLang is promising when prefix reuse and decode latency are important**, but its advantage depends more on workload shape.
>
> ## [doc:https://github.com/kaden-schutt/hipfire/blob/bfb90b9c822ec58c8f2ff1a0f01c3f4f0202c86d/docs/specs/2026-09-05-serving-cache-scheduler-spec.md] (doc) Shared-prefix serving: paged ownership, fair scheduling, and structured generation
> # Shared-prefix serving: paged ownership, fair scheduling, and structured generation
> ## 1. Decision
> 2. **SGLang/RadixAttention:** automatic longest-prefix lookup, retained prefix state, leaf-first eviction, and cache-aware scheduling.
> 4. **SGLang structured generation:** share compiled constraint machinery, keep parser state private, and use token-safe jump-forward for provably forced output.
>
> ### 1.1 Attribution and corrections to the motivating comparison
> - vLLM supports **automatic** prefix caching. Its current design uses chained block hashes; explicit/manual prefix registration is not required. A radix tree is an alternative index, not a capability vLLM categorically lacks.
> - SGLang's original API speculative execution generates beyond a stop boundary and reuses matching output for subsequent program primitives. It is not arbitrary speculative execution of side-effecting agent branches.
> - Neither prefix caching nor a serving scheduler changes the attention equation. Paged addressing must preserve the model's causal and positional semantics.
>
> Those records do not claim that general prefix caching originated here.
>
> ## 4. Prefix cache: exact state, not approximate prompt similarity
> ### 4.4 Completion and eviction — C4
> A synchronous implementation may retire at a proven step fence; later overlap cannot remove that proof.
>
> No copied stack-pointer kernargs or speculative reuse of staging storage.
>
> Keep useful ancestors while descendants use them. Reclaim cache-only pages before rejecting a new allocation.
>
> Cached prefixes and running requests share the same page pool. A cache-retention limit is a ceiling, not a permanently reserved VRAM partition. Running work has priority over cache-only residency. Idle-session and prefix-cache owners must not each believe the same bytes are exclusively theirs.
>

> ## [doc:https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/blob/fd6dc3dd2071ff3f067b5a3e33e9b8f1ac2f9818/docs/architecture/model-servers/sglang.md] (doc) SGLang in llm-d
> # SGLang in llm-d
> SGLang is a high-performance LLM serving engine featuring RadixAttention prefix caching, hierarchical KV caching (HiCache), and native prefill/decode disaggregation. In llm-d, SGLang operates as a first-class model server backend integrated with the router, KV-cache indexer, and disaggregated topologies.
>
> ## Pod Labeling & Discovery
>
> ## RadixAttention & KV-Cache Events
> SGLang manages KV-cache memory in a radix tree (`RadixAttention`), automatically reusing cached KV pages across shared system prompts, few-shot examples, and multi-turn chat histories.
>
> To enable cluster-wide prefix-cache affinity, SGLang publishes radix-tree insertion and eviction events over ZeroMQ when started with `--enable-kv-cache-events` and `--kv-events-config`. The KV-Cache Indexer consumes these events so the EPP can perform Precise Prefix-Cache Aware Routing.
>
> ## Prefill/Decode Disaggregation
> SGLang supports disaggregated prefill and decode pools coordinated through a prefill bootstrap server and the llm-d Routing Proxy Sidecar:
>
> - **Engine Mode & Transport:** Started with `--disaggregation-mode prefill` or `--disaggregation-mode decode` and `--disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl` (or `mooncake`), where the prefill worker pushes KV blocks to the decode worker over RDMA.
> - **Unconditional Disaggregation:** An SGLang decode worker (`--disaggregation-mode=decode`) requires every request to include bootstrap rendezvous fields and cannot fall back to local prefill. Deployments with SGLang therefore use `always-disagg-pd-decider` in the EPP.
>
> See Disaggregated Serving and SGLang Disaggregation Operations for details.
>

> ## [doc:https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/05ce0e980f00aa80864190d6f1cd5d9b685802f1/docs/cookbook/autoregressive/Google/EmbeddingGemma.mdx] (doc) EmbeddingGemma
> ## Deployment behavior
>
> EmbeddingGemma performs bidirectional attention over the complete input, so reusing a prefix KV cache or splitting the input into chunked prefills would produce incorrect attention states. SGLang applies the required settings automatically:
>
> - disables RadixAttention prefix caching;
> - disables chunked prefill;
> - disables the decode CUDA graph because this is an embedding-only model;
> - uses BCG for CUDA prefill;
> - uses the FlashAttention raw-K/V path when the prefill backend is FA3 or FA4 on supported Hopper and Blackwell CUDA GPUs.
>
> No prefill CUDA-graph override is required for this recipe. Keep BCG enabled to use the optimized EmbeddingGemma path.
> ```

> ## [doc:https://zeroentropy.dev/concepts/vllm-serving/] (doc) vLLM Serving
> # vLLM Serving
> Originating in Kwon et al. (2023, “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention”), vLLM stacks three core ideas — PagedAttention for KV-cache memory, continuous batching for compute, and prefix caching for prompt reuse — into a single serving engine that handles 2-10x more throughput than naive HuggingFace `generate()` on the same hardware (up to 24x on the original paper high-concurrency benchmarks).
>
> ## Why naive serving fails
> A transformer’s KV cache grows linearly with sequence length.
>
> ## PagedAttention: KV cache as virtual memory
> The cost is one indirection per attention computation — the GPU has to look up the block address before reading KV. vLLM’s custom CUDA kernel hides that latency well; the throughput gain from larger batches dominates.
>
> ## Prefix caching: reuse the system prompt
> If 1000 requests share the same 4K-token system prompt, naive serving recomputes the prefix’s KV 1000 times. vLLM’s prefix caching uses PagedAttention’s block-sharing to compute the prefix once and reuse it across all requests sharing it.
>
> In practice this is a 30-90% latency reduction on the first token (TTFT) for high-concurrency workloads with shared prompts — agent workloads, RAG with templated system messages, structured-output pipelines. See caching strategies for the broader cache hierarchy.
>
> ## What composes well on top
> - LoRA serving — multi-LoRA serving lets you serve hundreds of LoRA adapters from one base model with ~zero per-adapter overhead.
> - Quantization — AWQ, GPTQ, FP8, INT8 KV-cache quantization all integrate with PagedAttention.
>
> ## When vLLM is the wrong choice
> Secondary gotchas: prefix caching only helps if prefixes actually repeat (random prompts kill it), quantization can degrade quality on math-heavy or long-tail tasks, and multi-LoRA serving has per-adapter overhead at high QPS.
>
> ## Operational shape
> Memory KPI is KV-cache utilization (target ~90%+).
>
> ### vLLM vs TensorRT-LLM vs SGLang — when to use which?
> SGLang: faster prefix caching and structured-output decoding, smaller community.
>

> ## [doc:https://www.runpod.io/blog/run-vllm-on-runpod] (doc) Introduction to vLLM and PagedAttention
> # Introduction to vLLM and PagedAttention
> ## What is vLLM?
> Existing systems waste 60%-80% of the KV-Cache (LLM memory), whereas vLLM achieves near-optimal memory usage with a mere waste of under **4%**.
>
> ## What is PagedAttention, and how does it work?
> ### **Quantization**
> 8-bit quantization reduces the precision of the model's numerical data from the standard 32 bits to just 8 bits. Applying this technique to a large model like Llama 13B, for example, which initially requires 52 GB in a 32-bit format (13b*32 bits = 13b*4 bytes = 52GB), would now only need 13 GB post-quantization.
>
> This reduction in size allows models to fit better in memory, enabling a model like Llama 13B to run on a single 24 GB VRAM GPU. The process usually comes at the expense of some performance loss, but the tradeoff is worth the performance bump for many LLM inference use cases.
>
> ### **Automatic Prefix Caching**
> Improves efficiency by caching repeated computation across different inference requests, particularly beneficial in scenarios with repeated prompts​, including multi-round conversations.
>

>           "text": "# vLLM Serving\nOriginating in Kwon et al. (2023, “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention”), vLLM stacks three core ideas — PagedAttention for KV-cache memory, continuous batching for compute, and prefix caching for prompt reuse — into a single serving engine that handles 2-10x more throughput than naive HuggingFace `generate()` on the same hardware (up to 24x on the original paper high-concurrency benchmarks).\n\n## Why naive serving fails\nA transformer’s KV cache grows linearly with sequence length.\n\n## PagedAttention: KV cache as virtual memory\nThe cost is one indirection per attention computation — the GPU has to look up the block address before reading KV. vLLM’s custom CUDA kernel hides that latency well; the throughput gain from larger batches dominates.\n\n## Prefix caching: reuse the system prompt\nIf 1000 requests share the same 4K-token system prompt, naive serving recomputes the prefix’s KV 1000 times. vLLM’s prefix caching uses PagedAttention’s block-sharing to compute the prefix once and reuse it across all requests sharing it.\n\nIn practice this is a 30-90% latency reduction on the first token (TTFT) for high-concurrency workloads with shared prompts — agent workloads, RAG with templated system messages, structured-output pipelines. See caching strategies for the broader cache hierarchy.\n\n## What composes well on top\n- LoRA serving — multi-LoRA serving lets you serve hundreds of LoRA adapters from one base model with ~zero per-adapter overhead.\n- Quantization — AWQ, GPTQ, FP8, INT8 KV-cache quantization all integrate with PagedAttention.\n\n## When vLLM is the wrong choice\nSecondary gotchas: prefix caching only helps if prefixes actually repeat (random prompts kill it), quantization can degrade quality on math-heavy or long-tail tasks, and multi-LoRA serving has per-adapter overhead at high QPS.\n\n## Operational shape\nMemory KPI is KV-cache utilization (target ~90%+).\n\n### vLLM vs TensorRT-LLM vs SGLang — when to use which?\nSGLang: faster prefix caching and structured-output decoding, smaller community."

> ## [doc:https://github.com/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/blob/1553b52449a20eda8ddaa8fe742449d27039c0e2/docs/source/overview.md] (doc) Overview
> # Overview
> ## About TensorRT LLM
> TensorRT LLM is NVIDIA's comprehensive open-source library for accelerating and optimizing inference performance of the latest large language models (LLMs) on NVIDIA GPUs.
>
> ## Key Capabilities
> ### 🎯 **Comprehensive Model Support**
> TensorRT LLM strives to support the most popular models on **Day 0**.
>
> ### FP8 Support
> On NVIDIA H100 and later GPUs, TensorRT LLM supports FP8 quantization, which can double performance and halve memory consumption compared to 16-bit floating point, with minimal impact on model accuracy.
>
> ### 🚀 **Advanced Optimization & Production Features**
> - **In-Flight Batching & Paged Attention**: In-flight batching eliminates wait times by dynamically managing request execution, processing context and generation phases together for maximum GPU utilization and reduced latency.
> - **Speculative Decoding**: Multiple algorithms including EAGLE, MTP and NGram
> - **KV Cache Management**: Paged KV cache with intelligent block reuse and memory optimization
> - **Disaggregated Serving (Beta)**: Separate context and generation phases across different GPUs for optimal resource utilization
>
> ## What Can You Do With TensorRT LLM?
> To get started, refer to the {ref}`quick-start-guide`.
>

> ## Getting Started
> ### PyTorch Backend (LLM API)
> #### Clone TRT-LLM and set your model
> All keys in `model.yaml` map directly to `LLM()` constructor arguments. This is where you configure KV cache, quantization, parallelism, and more.
>
> ## Model Deployment
> ### Model Parallelism
> #### Tensor Parallelism, Pipeline Parallelism and Expert Parallelism
> Tensor Parallelism, and Expert parallelism
>
> With the LLM API, parallelism is configured directly in `model.yaml`; the keys map to the `LLM()` constructor arguments.
>
> Some examples are shown below:
>
> See the LLM API reference to learn more about how TensorRT-LLM supports expert parallelism in Mixture of Experts (MoE).
>
> ### Key-Value Cache
> See the KV Cache section for more details on how TensorRT-LLM supports KV cache. Also, check out the KV Cache Reuse documentation to learn more about how to enable KV cache reuse. KV cache options are configured through the LLM API in `model.yaml`.
>
> ### Decoding
> #### Speculative Decoding
> See the Speculative Decoding documentation to learn more about how TensorRT-LLM supports speculative decoding to improve the performance. The parameters for speculative decoding can be found in the model config of tensorrt_llm_bls model.
>
> ### Quantization
> Check out the Quantization Guide to learn more about how to install the quantization toolkit and quantize TensorRT-LLM models. Also, check out the blog post Speed up inference with SOTA quantization techniques in TRT-LLM to learn more about how to speed up inference with quantization.

> ## [doc:https://github.com/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/blob/1553b52449a20eda8ddaa8fe742449d27039c0e2/docs/source/blogs/tech_blog/blog05_Disaggregated_Serving_in_TensorRT-LLM.md] (doc) Disaggregated Serving in TensorRT LLM
> # Disaggregated Serving in TensorRT LLM
>
> By NVIDIA TensorRT LLM Team
>
> - Disaggregated Serving in TensorRT LLM
>   - Motivation
>   - Disaggregated Serving in TensorRT LLM

>   - Acknowledgement
>
> In the past tech blogs, we have introduced optimization specifically for low-latency and throughput oriented optimizations. For production deployment, users also care about per GPU throughput satisfying certain latency constraints. In this tech blog, we will introduce the design concept and usage of the TensorRT LLM disaggregated serving which directly targets throughput@latency performance scenarios, together with performance study results.
>
> ## [doc:https://github.com/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/blob/1553b52449a20eda8ddaa8fe742449d27039c0e2/docs/source/features/disagg-serving.md] (doc) Disaggregated Serving
> # Disaggregated Serving
>
> - Motivation
> - KV Cache Exchange
>   - Multi-backend Support
>   - Overlap Optimization
>   - Cache Layout Transformation
>   - Unique Global Request ID
> - Usage
>   - Dynamo
>   - trtllm-serve
>   - Multiple Instances
>   - Coordinator and Worker Fleet
> - Environment Variables
> - Troubleshooting and FAQ
>
> For the internals of the component that actually moves the KV blocks, see
> Introduction to KV Cache Transmission.
>
> For placing sub-agents with their parent while retaining independent conversation
> histories, see Sub-agent Routing.
>
> ## Motivation
>
> LLM inference has two stages: context (prefill) and generation (decode) phases. The context phase computes KV cache for prompt tokens whereas the generation phase generates tokens one by one using cached values. These phases have different compute characteristics.
>
> There are two ways of serving LLM inference requests:
>
> * Aggregated LLM serving (sometimes called in-flight batching or IFB in this tech blog), in which the context and generation phases are run on the same GPU.
> * Disaggregated LLM serving, in which the context and generation phases are run on different GPUs.
>
> Figure 1. The execution timeline of aggregated LLM serving
>
> In aggregated LLM serving, both the context and generation phases share the same GPU resources and parallelism strategy. This can lead to interference where context processing delays token generation, increasing token-to-token latency (TPOT) and reducing interactivity. This is illustrated in Figure 1 which shows the execution timeline for aggregated LLM serving. Aggregated LLM serving also forces a single GPU type and parallelism configuration for both phases, even though their compute needs differ. As a result, optimizing for one metric such as time-to-first-token (TTFT), often comes at the expense of another metric such as TPOT.

> # Speculative Decoding with TensorRT-LLM Backend
> ## Overview
> TensorRT-LLM backend provides highly optimized speculative decoding support for NVIDIA GPUs. This guide covers configuration and deployment of speculative decoding using the TensorRT-LLM backend.
>
> ## Documentation
> For comprehensive documentation on speculative decoding with TensorRT-LLM, please refer to the official TensorRT-LLM backend documentation:
>
> TensorRT-LLM Backend Decoding Documentation
>
> ## Key Features
> - Support for INT8/FP8 quantization
> - Advanced scheduling and batching
> - Medusa and standard speculative decoding modes
>
> ## Quick Reference
> For speculative decoding setup with TensorRT-LLM:
>
> 1. Build TensorRT-LLM engines for both target and draft models
>
> See the TensorRT-LLM backend documentation for detailed instructions.
>

> ## [doc:https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/blob/fd6dc3dd2071ff3f067b5a3e33e9b8f1ac2f9818/docs/architecture/model-servers/sglang.md] (doc) SGLang in llm-d
> ## RadixAttention & KV-Cache Events
>
> SGLang manages KV-cache memory in a radix tree (`RadixAttention`), automatically reusing cached KV pages across shared system prompts, few-shot examples, and multi-turn chat histories.
>
> To enable cluster-wide prefix-cache affinity, SGLang publishes radix-tree insertion and eviction events over ZeroMQ when started with `--enable-kv-cache-events` and `--kv-events-config`. The KV-Cache Indexer consumes these events so the EPP can perform Precise Prefix-Cache Aware Routing.
>
> ## Hierarchical KV Caching (HiCache)
>
> SGLang includes Hierarchical KV Caching (HiCache) to extend KV-cache capacity from GPU HBM into host CPU memory and external storage backends:
>
> - `--enable-hierarchical-cache`: Enables the host memory tier alongside the GPU radix cache.
> - `--hicache-ratio` / `--hicache-size`: Controls host KV-cache sizing relative to GPU capacity or as a fixed size.
> - `--hicache-write-policy`: Selects write-through or write-back caching behavior between GPU and host tiers.
> - `--hicache-storage-backend`: Connects an additional storage tier (such as filesystem or Mooncake).
>
> See KV Offloading and the Tiered Prefix Cache guide for architecture and deployment details.
>
> ## Prefill/Decode Disaggregation
>
> SGLang supports disaggregated prefill and decode pools coordinated through a prefill bootstrap server and the llm-d Routing Proxy Sidecar:
>
> - **Engine Mode & Transport:** Started with `--disaggregation-mode prefill` or `--disaggregation-mode decode` and `--disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl` (or `mooncake`), where the prefill worker pushes KV blocks to the decode worker over RDMA.
> - **Bootstrap Server Rendezvous:** Each prefill instance runs a bootstrap server (`--disaggregation-bootstrap-port 8998`). For each request, the Routing Proxy Sidecar (`--kv-connector=sglang`) generates a `bootstrap_room` ID and injects `bootstrap_host`, `bootstrap_port`, and `bootstrap_room` into the prefill and decode requests.
> - **Unconditional Disaggregation:** An SGLang decode worker (`--disaggregation-mode=decode`) requires every request to include bootstrap rendezvous fields and cannot fall back to local prefill. Deployments with SGLang therefore use `always-disagg-pd-decider` in the EPP.
>
> See Disaggregated Serving and SGLang Disaggregation Operations for details.
>

> ## [doc:https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/05ce0e980f00aa80864190d6f1cd5d9b685802f1/docs/docs/hardware-platforms/ascend-npus/model-deployment/tutorials/glm_5_2.mdx] (doc) GLM-5.2
> ## Introduction
>
> GLM-5.2 is a large language model in the GLM (General Language Model) series, jointly developed by the KEG Laboratory
> of Tsinghua University and Zhipu AI. GLM-5.2 adopts the DeepSeek-V3/V3.2 architecture, including DeepSeek Sparse
> Attention (DSA) and multi-token prediction (MTP), and supports high-throughput inference with SGLang on Ascend NPUs.
>
> This document demonstrates the deployment of GLM-5.2 on Ascend NPUs using SGLang, including single-node deployment,
> multi-node deployment, prefill-decode disaggregation, feature configuration, and performance optimization.
>
> ## Supported features
>
> | Feature                       | Example usage                                                                     |
> |-------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
> | Tensor Parallelism            | `--tp-size 16`                                                                    |
> | Data Parallelism              | `--dp-size 16`                                                                    |
> | Expert Parallelism            | `--ep-size 16 \``--moe-a2a-backend deepep \``--deepep-mode auto`         |
> | PD Disaggregation             | `--disaggregation-mode prefill \``--disaggregation-transfer-backend ascend`  |
> | Quantization                  | `--quantization modelslim`                                                        |
> | Chunked Prefill               | auto based on device memory, or set explicit value;disable with `--chunked-prefill-size -1`; e.g., `--chunked-prefill-size 16384` |
> | NPU Graph                     | enabled by default; disable with `--disable-cuda-graph`;control range via `--cuda-graph-bs-decode` or `--cuda-graph-max-bs-decode`; e.g., `--cuda-graph-bs-decode 16` |
> | Speculative Decoding          | `--speculative-algorithm NEXTN \``--speculative-num-steps 3 \``--speculative-eagle-topk 1 \``--speculative-num-draft-tokens 4 \``--speculative-draft-model-quantization unquant` |
> | Overlap Schedule              | `export SGLANG_ENABLE_OVERLAP_PLAN_STREAM=1`                                      |
> | DP LM Head                    | `--enable-dp-lm-head`                                                             |
>
> The values in the **Example usage** column are for illustration only. Adjust them according to your hardware, deployment
> mode, and workload. For parameter details, see
> Feature descriptions; for
> recommended configurations for each deployment scenario, see Best practices.
>
> For feature compatibility and conflict information between features,
> see Feature Compatibility.

>           "text": "Using Speculative Decoding with the SGLang backend.\n\nFor cross-backend documentation, see Speculative Decoding Overview.\n\n## Prerequisites\n\n- SGLang container or a local SGLang install. See the SGLang Backend guide.\n- One GPU for aggregated serving, two for disaggregated serving\n\n## Quick Start: Qwen3-8B + EAGLE3\n\nThis guide deploys **Qwen/Qwen3-8B** with the **Tengyunw/qwen3_8b_eagle3** EAGLE3 draft model.\n\n### Step 1: Start Infrastructure Services\n\n```bash\ndocker compose -f dev/docker-compose.yml up -d\n```\n\n### Step 2: Run Aggregated Speculative Decoding\n\n```bash\ncd examples/backends/sglang\n./launch/agg_spec_decoding.sh\n```\n\n### Step 3: Test the Deployment\n\n```bash\ncurl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \\\n  -H \"Content-Type: application/json\" \\\n  -d '{\n    \"model\": \"Qwen/Qwen3-8B\",\n    \"messages\": [\n      {\"role\": \"user\", \"content\": \"Write a poem about why Sakura trees are beautiful.\"}\n    ],\n    \"max_tokens\": 250\n  }'\n```\n… (41 more lines)",

>       "url": "https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/blob/fd6dc3dd2071ff3f067b5a3e33e9b8f1ac2f9818/docs/architecture/model-servers/sglang.md",
>       "title": "SGLang in llm-d",

>         {
>           "text": "## RadixAttention & KV-Cache Events\n\nSGLang manages KV-cache memory in a radix tree (`RadixAttention`), automatically reusing cached KV pages across shared system prompts, few-shot examples, and multi-turn chat histories.\n\nTo enable cluster-wide prefix-cache affinity, SGLang publishes radix-tree insertion and eviction events over ZeroMQ when started with `--enable-kv-cache-events` and `--kv-events-config`. The KV-Cache Indexer consumes these events so the EPP can perform Precise Prefix-Cache Aware Routing.\n\n## Hierarchical KV Caching (HiCache)\n\nSGLang includes Hierarchical KV Caching (HiCache) to extend KV-cache capacity from GPU HBM into host CPU memory and external storage backends:\n\n- `--enable-hierarchical-cache`: Enables the host memory tier alongside the GPU radix cache.\n- `--hicache-ratio` / `--hicache-size`: Controls host KV-cache sizing relative to GPU capacity or as a fixed size.\n- `--hicache-write-policy`: Selects write-through or write-back caching behavior between GPU and host tiers.\n- `--hicache-storage-backend`: Connects an additional storage tier (such as filesystem or Mooncake).\n\nSee KV Offloading and the Tiered Prefix Cache guide for architecture and deployment details.\n\n## Prefill/Decode Disaggregation\n\nSGLang supports disaggregated prefill and decode pools coordinated through a prefill bootstrap server and the llm-d Routing Proxy Sidecar:\n\n- **Engine Mode & Transport:** Started with `--disaggregation-mode prefill` or `--disaggregation-mode decode` and `--disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl` (or `mooncake`), where the prefill worker pushes KV blocks to the decode worker over RDMA.\n- **Bootstrap Server Rendezvous:** Each prefill instance runs a bootstrap server (`--disaggregation-bootstrap-port 8998`). For each request, the Routing Proxy Sidecar (`--kv-connector=sglang`) generates a `bootstrap_room` ID and injects `bootstrap_host`, `bootstrap_port`, and `bootstrap_room` into the prefill and decode requests.\n- **Unconditional Disaggregation:** An SGLang decode worker (`--disaggregation-mode=decode`) requires every request to include bootstrap rendezvous fields and cannot fall back to local prefill. Deployments with SGLang therefore use `always-disagg-pd-decider` in the EPP.\n\nSee Disaggregated Serving and SGLang Disaggregation Operations for details."
>         }

> ## [doc:https://unsloth.ai/docs/llms-full.txt] (doc) Vision Reinforcement Learning (VLM RL)
> # Vision Reinforcement Learning (VLM RL)
> Due to Unsloth's unique weight sharing and custom kernels, Unsloth makes VLM RL **1.5–2× faster,** uses **90% less VRAM**, and enables **15× longer context** lengths than FA2 setups, with no accuracy loss.
>
> We have also added vLLM VLM integration into Unsloth natively, so all you have to do to use vLLM inference is enable the `fast_inference=True` flag when initializing the model.
>
> This VLM support also integrates our latest update for even more memory efficient + faster RL including our Standby feature, which uniquely limits speed degradation compared to other implementations.
>
> You can only use `fast_inference` for VLMs supported by vLLM. Some models, like Llama 3.2 Vision thus only can run without vLLM, but they still work in Unsloth.
>

I restored `test.py` to your original code.

The problem is that this line:

```python
input_ids = tokenizer(input, return_tensors="pt").to(device)
```

does not make `input_ids` a tensor. The tokenizer returns a `BatchEncoding`, which is a dictionary-like object containing tensors:

```text
BatchEncoding
├── input_ids       -> Tensor shaped [batch_size, sequence_length]
└── attention_mask  -> Tensor shaped [batch_size, sequence_length]
```

Your model call works because you correctly extract the tensor:

```python
input_ids["input_ids"]
```

But here:

```python
torch.cat([input_ids, next_token_id], dim=-1)
```

the two values have different types:

```text
input_ids      -> BatchEncoding
next_token_id  -> Tensor
```

`torch.cat()` can concatenate only tensors, so it reports:

```text
expected Tensor as element 0, but got BatchEncoding
```

For this step, decide what the variable `input_ids` should represent. The clearest design is for it to contain only the actual token-ID tensor for the entire generation loop. Extract that tensor from the tokenizer result before entering the loop.

You can confirm the issue yourself by printing:

```python
print(type(input_ids))
print(type(input_ids["input_ids"]))
print(input_ids["input_ids"].shape)
print(next_token_id.shape)
```

The last two shapes should resemble:

```text
input_ids tensor:    [1, prompt_length]
next_token_id:       [1, 1]
```

Those are compatible for concatenation along `dim=-1`, producing `[1, prompt_length + 1]`.

One unrelated cleanup: naming the prompt variable `input` hides Python’s built-in `input()` function. It does not cause this error, but a name such as `prompt` will be clearer.

Step 5 is about splitting the generation process into two different operations:

```text
Prompt tokens ──prefill──> first-token logits + prompt KV cache
                                      │
                               sample first token
                                      │
New token + old cache ──decode──> next-token logits + updated cache
```

### What is wrong in your current `prefill()`

Your method currently calls the model twice:

```python
outputs = self.model(input_ids=input_ids, past_key_values=self.past_key_values)
...
outputs = self.model(input_ids=input_ids, past_key_values=self.past_key_values)
```

After the first call, the cache already represents the complete prompt. Sending the complete prompt again with that cache asks the model to process the prompt a second time.

There are also two scope problems:

- `prompt` does not exist inside `prefill()`.
- `device` is a global variable; the class already stores `self.device`.

Most importantly, this signature is conceptually incorrect:

```python
def decode(self, new_token, logits):
```

`decode()` does not need the previous logits. Logits are used by the sampler to choose `new_token`. What `decode()` needs is:

```text
new token + previous KV cache
```

### Function contracts

Design `prefill()` so that:

```text
Input:
    input_ids: [batch_size, prompt_length]

Output:
    next_token_logits: [batch_size, vocabulary_size]
    kv_cache: cache containing all prompt tokens
```

It should perform exactly one model call with the complete prompt and no old cache.

Design `decode()` so that:

```text
Input:
    new_token: [batch_size, 1]
    kv_cache: cache returned by prefill or the previous decode call

Output:
    next_token_logits: [batch_size, vocabulary_size]
    updated_kv_cache
```

It should perform exactly one model call and send only the new token—not the entire sequence. Hugging Face explicitly says that when `past_key_values` is supplied, `input_ids` should contain only tokens that have not already been processed. Its current default cache implementation is `DynamicCache`. [Hugging Face KV-cache guide](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/kv_cache)

### Correct execution order

For the prompt:

```text
"The capital of France is"
```

the flow should be:

```text
1. Tokenize the complete prompt
2. prefill(prompt_tokens)
3. Receive logits for the first generated token and prompt_cache
4. Sample token_1 from those logits
5. decode(token_1, prompt_cache)
6. Receive logits for token_2 and updated_cache
7. Sample token_2
8. decode(token_2, updated_cache)
9. Repeat
```

Notice an important detail: `prefill()` already gives you the logits used to select the first generated token. You should not decode anything before selecting that token.

### Shape walkthrough

Suppose the prompt has six tokens:

```text
prompt input_ids:        [1, 6]
prefill logits:          [1, vocabulary_size]
first sampled token:     [1, 1]
cache length:            6
```

After the first decode:

```text
decode input_ids:        [1, 1]
decode logits:           [1, vocabulary_size]
cache length:            7
```

After the second decode:

```text
decode input_ids:        [1, 1]
decode logits:           [1, vocabulary_size]
cache length:            8
```

```

Your expected input shapes are:

```

Keep the cache explicit—passed into and returned from the functions—instead of hiding it in `self.past_key_values`. That makes the data flow easier to understand now and will later allow different requests to own different caches.

`decode()` returns the logits for the following token, but you ignore them. Therefore, `logits` never changes, and line 43 repeatedly selects the same token from the original prefill logits.

What is already correct:

- `prefill()` processes the complete prompt once.
- `prefill()` produces logits for the first generated token.
- `decode()` receives only the newly generated token.
- `decode()` updates the KV cache.
- EOS is checked before another decode operation.
- Generated tokens are appended to the complete output sequence.

For the eventual inference engine, passing the cache explicitly would be cleaner:

```text
prefill(input_ids) -> logits, cache
decode(new_token, cache) -> logits, updated_cache
```

Your stateful `self.past_key_values` approach is acceptable for learning with one request, but it will not support several concurrent requests because each request needs its own cache.

> Explain step 6 a bit more

Step 6 is about separating “what the model predicts” from “how the engine chooses a token.”

The model does not directly return a token. It returns logits: one score for every token in the vocabulary.

For example:

```text
Token           Logit
" Paris"        14.2
" London"        8.1
" Berlin"        7.6
" France"        4.3
...
```

Greedy sampling simply selects the token with the highest logit.

### Tensor shapes

Your `prefill()` and `decode()` return:

```text
logits shape = [batch_size, vocabulary_size]
```

For one request and a vocabulary containing 150,000 tokens:

```text
[1, 150000]
```

Using:

```python
torch.argmax(logits, dim=-1, keepdim=True)
```

produces:

```text
next_token_id shape = [batch_size, 1]
```

For one request:

```text
[[token_id]]
```

`keepdim=True` is important because your existing sequence has shape:

```text
input_ids = [1, sequence_length]
```

The new token must have two dimensions so it can be concatenated:

```text
[1, sequence_length] + [1, 1]
```

Without `keepdim=True`, the result would be `[1]`, which is incompatible with the two-dimensional `input_ids`.

### Why softmax is unnecessary

You might expect sampling to require:

```python
probabilities = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
```

But greedy decoding only needs the largest value. Softmax does not change which value is largest:

```text
argmax(logits) == argmax(softmax(logits))
```

Therefore, applying softmax would do extra GPU work without changing the selected token.

### What the sampler should do

A sampler should have one responsibility:

```text
Input:  logits
Output: selected token IDs
```

It should not:

- Call the model
- Modify the KV cache
- Append tokens to a request
- Check EOS
- Decode tokens into text

Those responsibilities belong to the model runner and engine.

Conceptually:

```python
def greedy_sample(logits):
    # Choose the highest-scoring token for every batch row.
    # Return shape: [batch_size, 1]
```

Your current `torch.argmax(...)` already contains the main greedy-sampling operation. Step 6 asks you to move that operation into a clearly separated sampler and prove that it is correct.

### How generation flows

```text
prefill(prompt)
    ↓
logits for token 1
    ↓
greedy sampler selects token 1
    ↓
decode(token 1, cache)
    ↓
logits for token 2
    ↓
greedy sampler selects token 2
    ↓
decode(token 2, updated cache)
```

The sampled token becomes the input to the next decode call.

### How to verify it

Run two generation paths with exactly the same:

- Model
- Tokenizer
- Prompt token IDs
- `max_new_tokens`
- EOS token
- `do_sample=False`

Path one is your manual loop. Path two uses Hugging Face:

```text
model.generate(..., do_sample=False)
```

Compare generated token IDs, not only decoded text:

```text
Manual:      [785, 264, 9625, 13]
HuggingFace: [785, 264, 9625, 13]
```

Decoded strings can look identical even when their tokenization differs, so token IDs provide the stronger test.

Only compare the generated portion. Hugging Face returns:

```text
[prompt tokens] + [generated tokens]
```

If the prompt contains `P` tokens, the generated portion begins at position `P`.

### Why this test matters

If the token IDs differ, the sampler is not necessarily the problem. It could reveal an earlier error in:

- Selecting the wrong logits position
- Failing to update `logits` after `decode()`
- Passing the complete sequence during decode
- Reusing an old KV cache
- Using different tokenization
- Using sampling instead of greedy decoding

For your current code, Step 6 is complete when:

1. Greedy selection is moved into its own function or class.
2. It accepts `[batch_size, vocabulary_size]`.
3. It returns `[batch_size, 1]`.
4. `run()` uses the returned token.
5. Your generated token IDs match `model.generate(do_sample=False)`.

The idea of using `asyncio.Queue` is correct, but the current producer/consumer flow is not.

The first immediate issue is at [test.py:51](./test.py:51): `await` can only appear inside a function declared with `async def`. Your current `run()` is a normal function, so the file will raise a syntax error.

More importantly, these two lines cancel the purpose of the queue:

```python
await queue.put(self.greedy_sample(logits))
next_token_id = await queue.get()
```

The same function puts a token into the queue and immediately removes it. Nothing is being streamed to another consumer.

### The intended architecture

There should be two independent pieces:

```text
Generation producer              API consumer
-------------------              ------------
Generate token
Put token in queue  ────────────> Wait for token
Continue decoding                 Read and send token
Generate next token               Wait for next token
Put token in queue  ────────────> Read and send token
```

The generation loop should only put tokens into the queue. It should never retrieve them.

The API or a separate streaming function should retrieve them.

### Queue ownership

Your queue is currently created inside `run()`:

```python
queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=10)
```

That means the API cannot access it. Eventually, every `Request` should own an output queue:

```text
Request
├── request_id
├── prompt_token_ids
├── output_token_ids
├── status
└── output_queue
```

For this learning step, you can instead create the queue outside `run()` and pass it into both:

- The generation producer
- The streaming consumer

### Keep using the sampled token directly

After sampling:

```text
next_token_id = greedy_sample(logits)
```

the producer should do two separate things with it:

```text
1. Put it into the output queue for the consumer.
2. Pass it to decode() to continue generation.
```

It should not retrieve the token from the queue before calling `decode()`.

### You need a completion signal

When generation finishes, the consumer may be waiting at:

```python
token = await queue.get()
```

It needs a way to know that no more tokens are coming. A common approach is to insert a sentinel value such as `None`:

```text
token
token
token
None    ← generation has finished
```

The consumer stops when it receives the sentinel.

Put the completion signal into the queue whether generation:

- Produces EOS
- Reaches `max_new_tokens`
- Is cancelled
- Fails with an exception

Eventually, an output event object is cleaner than using `None`, because it can represent token, completion and error events.

### Avoid placing GPU tensors in the queue

Your current sampler returns a tensor located on the model’s device:

```text
Tensor([[1234]], device="mps")
```

Leaving GPU tensors inside an output queue can keep GPU memory alive unnecessarily. An API consumer also does not need a GPU tensor.

The queue should normally contain:

- A Python token ID
- A CPU token tensor
- Or, after Step 9, a decoded text piece

For Step 8, a Python integer token ID is sufficient.

### Queue size matters

This queue is bounded:

```python
asyncio.Queue(maxsize=10)
```

After ten unread tokens, `await queue.put(...)` waits for the consumer. That is backpressure, but it also pauses the generation producer.

For this first implementation, an unbounded queue is simpler. Later, you must choose between:

- A bounded queue that slows generation when the client is slow
- An unbounded queue that could grow if the client stops reading
- Cancelling requests whose clients are too slow or disconnected

### Desired control flow

Your target is:

```text
1. Create output queue.
2. Start generation as a producer task.
3. Producer performs prefill.
4. Producer samples a token.
5. Producer stores the token locally.
6. Producer puts a streamable copy into the queue.
7. Producer checks stopping conditions.
8. Producer passes the local token directly to decode().
9. Consumer independently reads queue entries.
10. Producer sends a completion sentinel when finished.
```

Also notice that [test.py:72](./test.py:72) currently calls `model.run(...)` like a normal function. If `run()` becomes asynchronous, the caller must run or await that coroutine.

One unrelated issue: [test.py:24](./test.py:24) ignores the constructor’s `max_new_tokens` argument and always sets it to `100`.

So: the queue is the right tool, but you still need to separate the generation producer from the streaming consumer.

For Step 8 only, structure it as one producer and one consumer:

```python
import asyncio
import torch

STREAM_END = None

class Model:
    def __init__(self, model_name, device, max_new_tokens):
        self.model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
            model_name,
            use_cache=True,
        )

        self.device = device
        self.max_new_tokens = max_new_tokens

        self.model.to(self.device)
        self.model.eval()

        self.tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
        self.past_key_values = None

    def prefill(self, input_ids):
        outputs = self.model(
            input_ids=input_ids,
            past_key_values=None,
            use_cache=True,
        )

        self.past_key_values = outputs.past_key_values
        return outputs.logits[:, -1, :]

    def decode(self, new_token):
        outputs = self.model(
            input_ids=new_token,
            past_key_values=self.past_key_values,
            use_cache=True,
        )

        self.past_key_values = outputs.past_key_values
        return outputs.logits[:, -1, :]

    def greedy_sample(self, logits):
        return torch.argmax(
            logits,
            dim=-1,
            keepdim=True,
        )

    async def run(self, prompt, output_queue):
        self.past_key_values = None

        input_ids = self.tokenizer(
            prompt,
            return_tensors="pt",
        ).to(self.device)["input_ids"]

        generated_tokens = 0

        try:
            with torch.inference_mode():
                logits = self.prefill(input_ids)

                while generated_tokens < self.max_new_tokens:
                    next_token = self.greedy_sample(logits)
                    next_token_id = next_token.item()

                    input_ids = torch.cat(
                        [input_ids, next_token],
                        dim=-1,
                    )

                    generated_tokens += 1

                    # Producer sends the token to the consumer.
                    output_queue.put_nowait(next_token_id)

                    # Give the consumer a chance to process it.
                    await asyncio.sleep(0)

                    if next_token_id == self.tokenizer.eos_token_id:
                        break

                    logits = self.decode(next_token)

        finally:
            # Tell the consumer that generation has finished.
            output_queue.put_nowait(STREAM_END)

        return input_ids
```

The consumer is separate:

```python
async def consume_tokens(output_queue):
    while True:
        token_id = await output_queue.get()

        if token_id is STREAM_END:
            break

        print("Received token:", token_id)

        output_queue.task_done()
```

Run the producer and consumer together:

```python
async def main():
    model_name = "Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B"

    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        device = "cuda"
    elif torch.backends.mps.is_available():
        device = "mps"
    else:
        device = "cpu"

    model = Model(
        model_name=model_name,
        device=device,
        max_new_tokens=100,
    )

    output_queue = asyncio.Queue()

    generation_task = asyncio.create_task(
        model.run(
            prompt="The capital of France is",
            output_queue=output_queue,
        )
    )

    await consume_tokens(output_queue)

    complete_input_ids = await generation_task

    print(
        model.tokenizer.decode(
            complete_input_ids[0],
            skip_special_tokens=True,
        )
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

The important separation is:

```text
run()               consume_tokens()
-----               ----------------
Generates token
Puts token in queue
Continues decoding  Gets token from queue
                    Sends or prints token
```

The error occurs because `Model.run()` does not return anything.

At [test.py:86](./test.py:86), awaiting `generation_task` gives you the value returned by `run()`. Since `run()` reaches its end without an explicit return, Python returns `None`.

Therefore:

- `complete_input_ids` becomes `None`.
- `complete_input_ids[0]` attempts to index `None`.
- Python raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable`.

Printing the decoded result at [test.py:63](./test.py:63) does not return it. `run()` should explicitly return the completed `input_ids` after the `finally` block.

There is also a separate streaming issue: no generated token is currently placed into `output_queue`. The only queue entry is `STREAM_END` in the `finally` block. Consequently, `consume_tokens()` receives no tokens and immediately finishes when generation ends.

After sampling each token, the producer should:

1. Keep the tensor locally for `decode()`.
2. Extract its integer token ID.
3. Put that integer into `output_queue`.
4. Yield control so the consumer can run.
5. Check EOS.
6. Continue decoding if generation has not finished.

The completion sentinel in `finally` is correctly placed because it guarantees that the consumer is notified even if generation fails.

Also, `self.queue` at [test.py:31](./test.py:31) is unused. Your code uses the separate `output_queue` created in `main()`. Keep one ownership design rather than maintaining both.

> Explain step 9 more

Step 9 converts the token IDs from Step 8 into text chunks that can safely be shown to the user.

The important problem is that one token does not always equal one complete word or character.

For example, “Paris” might be represented as:

- Token 1: `" Par"`
- Token 2: `"is"`

Unicode characters can be more difficult. An emoji or accented character may depend on multiple tokens. Decoding each token separately can therefore produce broken characters, missing spaces, or replacement symbols.

### State needed for each request

Keep these two values:

- `generated_token_ids`: every generated token ID so far
- `emitted_text`: the text already sent to the client

Do not use the complete prompt tokens for this. Usually, a generation API streams only newly generated text.

### Processing each new token

Whenever the sampler produces a token:

1. Convert its ID from a GPU tensor into a normal integer.
2. Append it to `generated_token_ids`.
3. Decode the complete `generated_token_ids` list.
4. Compare the newly decoded text with `emitted_text`.
5. Extract only the text that appears after `emitted_text`.
6. Put that new text portion into the output queue.
7. Update `emitted_text`.

Suppose the request has produced these tokens:

```text
Token 1 → decoded sequence: "The"
Token 2 → decoded sequence: "The capital"
Token 3 → decoded sequence: "The capital of"
```

The streamed pieces should be:

```text
"The"
" capital"
" of"
```

You should not send the complete decoded sequence after every token, because the client would receive repeated text:

```text
"The"
"The capital"
"The capital of"
```

### Why decoding only the newest token is unreliable

A tokenizer may use information from neighbouring tokens to reconstruct text correctly.

For example, separate token decoding might give:

```text
Token A → "hello"
Token B → "world"
```

But decoding both together might produce:

```text
"hello world"
```

The space may be encoded as part of a tokenization rule rather than appearing cleanly when each token is decoded alone.

The same issue occurs with:

- Emoji
- Accented characters
- Chinese, Japanese and Korean text
- Newlines
- Leading spaces
- Punctuation
- Code indentation
- Tokens representing partial UTF-8 bytes

Decoding the complete generated sequence each time gives the tokenizer enough context.

### Where it belongs in your flow

The order should be:

1. Sample the next token.
2. Save the token ID in the request.
3. Decode the growing generated-token list.
4. Find the new text portion.
5. Put that portion into the output queue.
6. Check whether the token is EOS.
7. Continue with `decode()` if generation is not finished.

The output queue should now contain text pieces rather than GPU tensors.

Your engine must still keep token IDs separately because they are needed for:

- Model decoding
- Stop-token checks
- Repetition penalties
- Correctness tests
- Usage statistics

### EOS handling

EOS is a control token and normally should not appear in the streamed text.

When EOS is produced:

1. Add it to the internal token history if needed.
2. Decode with special tokens excluded.
3. Send any remaining unsent text.
4. Send the stream-completion event.
5. Do not send a literal EOS string.

### Unstable trailing text

Sometimes the last token sequence is not yet safely decodable. The decoded result might temporarily end with the replacement character `�`. A later token can complete the character and replace it with the correct text.

For the first version, you can keep the logic simple:

- Do not emit a new suffix containing an incomplete replacement character.
- Keep it pending.
- Decode again after the next token arrives.
- Emit it when it becomes valid.
- Flush any valid remaining text when generation finishes.

### Performance trade-off

Decoding the complete generated list after every token repeatedly processes old tokens. That is not ideal for a production engine, but it is a good first implementation because correctness is easier to understand and test.

Later, you can create a dedicated incremental detokenizer that keeps a small token buffer and decodes only the unstable tail.

### Tests for Step 9

Test prompts that generate:

- Normal sentences
- Spaces before words
- Commas and periods
- Multiple lines
- Code with indentation
- Emoji
- Accented characters
- Non-English text
- EOS immediately after some text

For every test, joining all streamed text pieces should exactly equal decoding the complete generated-token list once at the end. That equality is the main correctness condition for Step 9.

Think of Step 9 as this:

- Step 8 streams token IDs, such as `927`, `462`, `13`.
- Step 9 converts those token IDs into readable text pieces.

The confusing part is: you should not decode only the newest token. Instead, decode all generated tokens so far, then send only the part the user has not already seen.

Example:

| New token arrives | Decode all generated tokens | Text already sent | Send now |
|---|---|---|---|
| Token 1 | `" Par"` | `""` | `" Par"` |
| Token 2 | `" Paris"` | `" Par"` | `"is"` |
| Token 3 | `" Paris is"` | `" Paris"` | `" is"` |
| Token 4 | `" Paris is beautiful"` | `" Paris is"` | `" beautiful"` |

Your request therefore needs to remember two things:

1. All generated token IDs.
2. How much decoded text has already been sent.

The flow for every generated token is:

1. Generate a token ID.
2. Add it to the list of generated token IDs.
3. Decode the entire generated list.
4. Remove the text already sent.
5. Put only the remaining new text into the queue.
6. Remember the complete decoded text as “already sent.”

For example:

```text
Previously sent:
" Paris"

New complete decoded text:
" Paris is"

New portion:
" is"
```

Only `" is"` goes into the queue.

Why not decode just the newest token? Because some tokens are only pieces of text. Two tokens might separately look incomplete but together form a valid word, emoji, or character.

The final correctness rule is simple:

```text
streamed piece 1
+ streamed piece 2
+ streamed piece 3
= final decoded generated text
```

For Step 9, change the queue’s meaning:

```text
Step 8 queue:
token IDs

Step 9 queue:
new text pieces
```

Keep the token IDs inside the request for model generation, but send text pieces to the API/user.

|---|---|---|---|

| `[100, 200]` | `"The capital"` | `"The"` | `" capital"` |
| `[100, 200, 300]` | `"The capital is"` | `"The capital"` | `" is"` |

Closer, but Step 9 is not correct yet. There are five issues.

1. Wrong object performs text decoding

At [test.py:62](./test.py:62), you call `decode` on `self.model`.

The language model produces logits; it does not convert token IDs into text. Text decoding belongs to `self.tokenizer`.

2. You are decoding only the newest token

You currently try to decode `next_token_id`. Step 9 requires decoding `generated_token_ids`, the complete list you correctly maintain at [test.py:50](./test.py:50).

The responsibilities are:

- `next_token_id` tensor goes into the model’s `decode()`.
- `generated_token_ids` list goes into the tokenizer’s `decode()`.

3. You are not tracking text already sent

You need another value initialized before the loop: the complete text already sent to the consumer.

After every new token:

- Decode all `generated_token_ids`.
- Compare that result with the text already sent.
- Extract only the new ending.
- Queue that new ending.
- Update the text-already-sent value.

Without this state, you either send broken individual tokens or repeatedly send the complete response.

4. `output_queue.put()` is asynchronous

At [test.py:62](./test.py:62), calling `put()` creates a coroutine, but you neither await it nor schedule it. The item is therefore not actually placed into the queue.

You must either wait for the asynchronous put operation or use the immediate queue operation. If you use the immediate operation, the producer must still yield control after queueing so the consumer can run.

5. Producer and consumer are running sequentially

At [test.py:88](./test.py:88), you wait for generation to finish before starting `consume_tokens()` at line 89.

That is not streaming. The intended order is:

1. Start the generation task.
2. Immediately start consuming its queue.
3. The producer and consumer operate together.
4. After the consumer receives `STREAM_END`, await the generation task to collect any final result or exception.

Your intended per-token flow should be:

```text
Sample next_token_id
        ↓
Append its integer ID to generated_token_ids
        ↓
Decode all generated_token_ids using the tokenizer
        ↓
Subtract text already sent
        ↓
Put only the new text into output_queue
        ↓
Yield control to the consumer
        ↓
Check EOS
        ↓
Pass next_token_id tensor into model decode()
```

The `STREAM_END` placement inside `finally` is correct. The unused `self.queue` at [test.py:31](./test.py:31) can also be removed later because the queue from `main()` is the one actually being used.

Your `run()` loop should follow this shape:

```python
async def run(self, prompt, output_queue):
    self.past_key_values = None

    input_ids = self.tokenizer(
        prompt,
        return_tensors="pt",
    ).to(self.device)["input_ids"]

    generated_token_ids = []
    emitted_text = ""

    try:
        with torch.inference_mode():
            logits = self.prefill(input_ids)

            while len(generated_token_ids) < self.max_new_tokens:
                # Tensor shaped [1, 1].
                next_token_id = self.greedy_sample(logits)

                # Convert it to a normal integer for text handling.
                token_id = next_token_id.item()
                generated_token_ids.append(token_id)

                # Decode every generated token so far.
                current_text = self.tokenizer.decode(
                    generated_token_ids,
                    skip_special_tokens=True,
                    clean_up_tokenization_spaces=False,
                )

                # Remove the text that was already streamed.
                new_text = current_text[len(emitted_text):]

                if new_text:
                    await output_queue.put(new_text)
                    emitted_text = current_text

                # Allow the consumer to run now.
                await asyncio.sleep(0)

                if token_id == self.tokenizer.eos_token_id:
                    break

                # The model receives only the latest token tensor.
                logits = self.decode(next_token_id)

    finally:
        await output_queue.put(STREAM_END)
```

Notice the two different decoding operations:

```python
# Model decoding: generate the next logits.
logits = self.decode(next_token_id)

# Tokenizer decoding: convert IDs into readable text.
current_text = self.tokenizer.decode(generated_token_ids)
```

They are unrelated despite both using the word “decode.”

Your consumer should now expect text, not token IDs:

```python
async def consume_tokens(output_queue):
    while True:
        text_chunk = await output_queue.get()

        if text_chunk is STREAM_END:
            output_queue.task_done()
            break

        print(text_chunk, end="", flush=True)
        output_queue.task_done()
```

In `main()`, do not wait for generation before starting the consumer:

```python
generation_task = asyncio.create_task(
    model.run(
        prompt=prompt,
        output_queue=output_queue,
    )
)

await consume_tokens(output_queue)
await generation_task
```

The important line is:

```python
new_text = current_text[len(emitted_text):]
```

For example:

```text
emitted_text = " Paris"
current_text = " Paris is"
new_text     = " is"
```

Only `" is"` is placed in the queue. Afterward:

```text
emitted_text = " Paris is"
```

Then the next iteration might produce:

```text
current_text = " Paris is beautiful"
new_text     = " beautiful"
```

Also remove your current line that calls `self.model.decode(...)`. The tokenizer converts IDs to text; the model object does not have that responsibility.

I verified the behavior using the same Python 3.12 environment from your traceback.

For Qwen3, tokenizing an empty string produces:

- Shape: `[1, 0]`
- Data type: `float32`
- Token IDs: none

Qwen3’s tokenizer also has no configured BOS token:

- `tokenizer.bos_token_id` is `None`
- `model.config.bos_token_id` is `151643`

### Why this error happens

The embedding layer expects integer token IDs. With a normal prompt, the tokenizer creates an integer tensor because it has integer values.

For an empty prompt, the tokenizer creates an empty tensor. Because there are no values from which to infer the type, it becomes a floating-point tensor on MPS.

The embedding layer then rejects it:

```text
Embedding input:
empty MPS float tensor

Expected:
integer token-ID tensor
```

Simply converting the empty tensor to integers is not enough. You would then have an integer tensor with shape `[1, 0]`, meaning there are still no tokens to process. Your prefill method could not select the last-token logits because no last token exists.

### You have two valid policies

#### Option 1: Reject empty prompts

This is the simplest policy for your first engine version.

Immediately after tokenization, check whether the sequence length is zero. If it is, mark the request as invalid with a clear message such as “prompt must contain at least one token.”

This is a good first implementation because it avoids model-specific start-token behavior.

#### Option 2: Insert a start token

If you want to support empty prompts, your engine must give the model one artificial starting token.

For this Qwen3 model, use the model configuration’s BOS token ID, not the tokenizer’s BOS token ID:

```text
tokenizer.bos_token_id    → None
model.config.bos_token_id → 151643
```

Create a one-token input with:

- Value: `model.config.bos_token_id`
- Shape: `[1, 1]`
- Data type: integer/long
- Device: the model’s device

The start token is only internal input. Do not add it to `generated_token_ids`, and do not stream it to the user.

The flow becomes:

```text
User prompt: ""
    ↓
Tokenizer returns no tokens
    ↓
Engine inserts model BOS token
    ↓
Prefill receives one integer token
    ↓
Model produces logits for the first generated token
```

### Do not hardcode `151643`

Read the value from `model.config.bos_token_id`. Other models use different start-token IDs, and some models may not define one at all.

If both the tokenizer and model configurations lack a BOS token, your engine should reject the empty prompt unless you deliberately define a model-specific fallback.

### One related Qwen3 detail

Your current stopping logic checks only `tokenizer.eos_token_id`, which is `151645`.

However, Qwen3’s generation configuration defines two valid stopping tokens:

```text
151645
151643
```

Eventually, your stopping logic should support a collection of EOS IDs rather than assuming there is exactly one.

For your first engine version, I recommend supporting empty prompts by inserting `model.config.bos_token_id`. This lets you keep the empty-prompt test from your design document while still giving prefill a valid token.
