> Now step 3

Step 3 is about keeping **decode responsive while prefill work is happening**. Your scheduler already does the first half: in [scheduler.py](./utils/scheduler.py:25), it counts each running decode request as one token *before* giving the remaining budget to prefill chunks.

The missing half is execution order. [Engine.step()](./utils/engine.py:176) runs prefill first. If that prefill is slow, a request ready to produce its next token still waits.

The intended flow is:

```text
scheduler selects decode requests and prefill chunks
check the blocks needed for all selected work

run decode batch
update requests and put new text in their output queues

give the async output consumers a chance to run

run prefill batch
advance each prompt cursor
generate a token only for prompts that just finished
```

There is a subtlety: merely moving the decode code above prefill inside the synchronous `step()` improves *GPU execution order*, but `run()` currently yields to asyncio only **after the entire step**. A streaming consumer may therefore still wait for prefill to finish before it can read the queued text. For this step, I’d keep the scheduler’s decode-first budget rule, process decode first, and arrange an async yield between decode and prefill. Tests should verify both that decode gets budget and that a decode result becomes available before a long prefill phase completes.

> Suggestions for how to yield between the decode and prefill processing in Engine.step?

You can’t yield *inside* the current synchronous `Engine.step()`—`await asyncio.sleep(0)` requires an `async` function.

I’d split the work into reusable phases, while keeping `step()` synchronous for your existing tests:

```text
schedule_step()       → SchedulerOutput and capacity check
process_decode(...)   → model call, update requests, queue text
process_prefill(...)  → model call, advance prompt cursors
```

Then use those phases in two ways:

```text
step():                     # existing synchronous test interface
    work = schedule_step()
    process_decode(work)
    process_prefill(work)
    return whether work remains

async run():                # streaming interface
    while work remains:
        work = schedule_step()
        process_decode(work)
        await asyncio.sleep(0)   # queued decode text can be consumed here
        process_prefill(work)
        await asyncio.sleep(0)
```

This avoids duplicating the generation logic or converting all your `step()` tests to async. One safeguard: a request might be cancelled while `run()` is yielding, so `process_prefill()` should skip any scheduled request that is no longer in `PREFILL`.

> What about the last line in the step function - where I filter out the finished or cancelled requests?

Move that filtering into a small helper, then call it **after each phase**—especially before the async yield:

```text
work = schedule_step()

process_decode(work)
remove_finished_and_cancelled_from_scheduler_running()
await asyncio.sleep(0)

process_prefill(work)   # skip requests cancelled during the yield
remove_finished_and_cancelled_from_scheduler_running()
await asyncio.sleep(0)

return bool(scheduler.waiting or scheduler.running)
```

The synchronous `step()` calls the same phases and cleanup helper, just without the yields. Keep its `return bool(...)` **after the final cleanup**, as it is now; otherwise a finished request still in `running` could make the engine think work remains.

You’re right—I’ve removed only the edits I made in this interrupted turn. Your earlier `Engine` phase split and its tests are intact.

The issue is the order in [schedule_step()](./utils/engine.py:209):

```text
scheduler.schedule()  → moves a waiting request into running/PREFILL
check free KV blocks  → may raise an error
```

If the check raises, the request has already left `waiting`, even though no prompt tokens were processed. On the next attempt, the scheduler sees it as a running prefill request. That is the inconsistent state we want to prevent.

I suggest separating **planning** from **committing**:

```text
Scheduler.plan():
    calculate decode requests and prefill chunk lengths
    record which waiting requests would be admitted
    do not pop waiting, append running, or change any status
    return SchedulerOutput

Engine.schedule_step():
    output = scheduler.plan()
    calculate blocks needed for output

    if blocks are insufficient:
        raise KVCacheExhaustedError
        # queues and statuses are still unchanged

    scheduler.commit(output)
    return output

Scheduler.commit(output):
    for each newly admitted waiting request:
        change WAITING → PREFILL
        remove it from waiting
        add it to running
```

The key distinction is that continuing `PREFILL` requests are already in `running`; `commit()` should move **only newly admitted** requests. You can store those separately in `SchedulerOutput`, alongside the existing `prefill_requests` and `prefill_token_counts`.

To preserve your current scheduler tests, `schedule()` can remain a convenience method that calls `plan()` followed by `commit()`. The engine should use the two calls separately so it can check capacity between them.

Test the failure case with a full one-block cache: add a waiting request, call `engine.step()` and expect `KVCacheExhaustedError`, then assert the request is still `WAITING`, still in `scheduler.waiting`, absent from `running`, and has `num_computed_tokens == 0`.

Step 4 is **admission control**: before moving a request from `waiting` to `running`, decide whether its first prefill chunk fits in the KV cache *without using memory you want to keep available for requests already running*.

You already have the first part in [Engine.schedule_step()](./utils/engine.py:208): it calculates the blocks needed for this step. Right now, though, [Scheduler.plan()](./utils/scheduler.py:21) admits waiting requests first, and the engine raises `KVCacheExhaustedError` if the resulting plan is too large. Step 4 changes that decision: a new request that does not fit should **stay waiting**, while work that *does* fit can proceed.

A simple first policy is to reserve one spare block per *existing running request*. That is conservative, but easy to reason about:

```text
At the start of planning:
    free_blocks = blocks currently free in the KV cache

Plan work for running requests:
    calculate blocks needed for their scheduled decode/prefill
    subtract that cost from free_blocks

Reserve headroom:
    reserved_blocks = number of existing running requests

For each waiting request, in order:
    calculate its first prefill chunk using the remaining token budget
    candidate_blocks = blocks needed for that chunk

    if free_blocks - candidate_blocks < reserved_blocks:
        stop admitting requests; leave this request in waiting

    add the request and chunk to the plan
    free_blocks -= candidate_blocks
    increment num_admitted_requests

After the plan is accepted:
    commit the admitted requests
    execute the batches
```

For a new request with no blocks yet, `candidate_blocks` is approximately `ceil(chunk_length / block_size)`. For requests that already have a block table, use the same “blocks needed” calculation you currently use in `schedule_step()`, so you do not count existing blocks twice.

Keep the **plan → check → commit** separation you just built. Admission decisions belong in planning; `commit()` should still be the point where waiting requests actually change state. You’ll need to give the planner the cache information it lacks today—at least free-block count and block size—or have the engine perform the admission portion before committing.

One important boundary: if *running requests alone* cannot fit, admission control cannot solve that. Leave that for step 5, recompute preemption. Also avoid an endless loop when there are waiting requests but no running request that could ever free memory; that situation needs an explicit capacity error rather than repeated empty steps.

I’d test three cases: a new request fits and is admitted; it does not fit and remains waiting while an existing request progresses; and it becomes admissible after the running request finishes and frees its blocks.

> How do I handle this logic:
> If no new request was admitted:
>     if a running request has scheduled decode or prefill work:
>         return the plan normally
>
>     if no work is scheduled but requests are waiting:
>         first see whether a smaller prefill chunk could fit

The key is to **shrink the chunk inside the waiting-request loop**, then decide whether the *whole plan* has work. Don’t use `i == 0` as the error condition: `i` counts new admissions, not scheduled decode or prefill.

In [Scheduler.plan()](./utils/scheduler.py), after subtracting the blocks needed by running requests:

```text
For the next waiting request:
    blocks_available_for_admission = max(0, free_blocks - reserved_blocks)
    tokens_that_fit_in_cache = blocks_available_for_admission * block_size

    chunk_len = minimum of:
        remaining prompt tokens
        prefill chunk size
        remaining token budget
        tokens_that_fit_in_cache

    if chunk_len == 0:
        leave this request waiting; stop admitting

    add this chunk to the plan
    subtract its blocks from free_blocks
    increment the admission count
```

That token-capacity calculation works for your *current* waiting requests because their block tables are empty.

Then, **after the loop**, replace the `if i == 0` check with this decision:

```text
if the plan contains any decode request or prefill request:
    return the plan normally

if requests are waiting but the plan contains no work:
    raise a capacity error

otherwise:
    return the empty plan  # the engine has nothing to do
```

For example, if one request is decoding and another cannot fit, the plan still contains decode work—return it. If the engine has only a waiting request and zero free blocks, the plan contains no work and cannot progress—raise. If it has one free block of size 2 and a four-token prompt, schedule a **two-token chunk** instead of rejecting the request.

Step 5 is **recompute preemption**. When the work selected for a step needs more KV blocks than are free, pause one running request, free its cache blocks, and rebuild its cache later from its tokens. The request is *not* cancelled: its generated text and output queue stay intact.

The important detail in your engine is that a decoding request’s **latest generated token has not entered the KV cache yet**. For example:

```text
Original prompt:       [A, B]
Generated so far:      [X, Y]
Currently cached:      [A, B, X]
Next decode input:      Y
```

If you preempt this request, its recompute prefill must rebuild `[A, B, X]`. It must **not generate another token** at the end of that prefill. The following decode step feeds `Y` and generates the next token normally.

I’d implement it in this order:

1. Add a request transition such as `preempt_for_recompute()`. It changes the status to `WAITING` and resets `num_computed_tokens` to `0`. Preserve `prompt_token_ids`, `generated_token_ids`, `emitted_text`, and the output queue. Have the engine free the request’s block table using its existing cache-release method.
2. Give the request a way to expose the tokens to prefill: normally its original prompt; after decoding has begun, `original prompt + generated tokens except the latest one`. Keep the original `prompt_token_ids` unchanged—it is also used to report the original prompt length.
3. Make [Scheduler.plan()](./utils/scheduler.py), [PrefillBatch](./utils/batch.py), and the request’s prefill-completion checks use that prefill-token sequence.
4. In [Engine.process_prefill_batch()](./utils/engine.py:186), distinguish ordinary prefill from recompute. On completing recompute, transition to decoding **without sampling or streaming** a token.
5. In [Engine.schedule_step()](./utils/engine.py:209), replace the immediate capacity error with a bounded retry:

```text
plan the step
if its required blocks fit:
    commit and return the plan

choose a running request to preempt
if there is no suitable victim:
    raise the capacity error

free that request’s blocks and move it to waiting
plan again
```

For a first victim policy, choose the **most recently admitted running request** (`running[-1]`), and keep the choice deterministic. Don’t repeatedly preempt and readmit the same sole request: if no request can make progress, raise an error instead of looping forever.

The first tests I’d write are: preempt during chunked prefill; preempt after two generated tokens and verify no token is emitted twice; verify blocks are freed; and verify an impossible-to-fit request fails rather than spinning.

> Explain with more pseudocode

The tricky part is that **preempting a request means throwing away its KV cache, not throwing away its progress or output**. I’d split the implementation into three small pieces.

### 1. Record what must be rebuilt

In [Request](./utils/request.py), keep the original `prompt_token_ids` unchanged. Add a flag meaning “after recompute, resume decoding.”

```text
prefill_tokens(request):
    if request must resume decoding:
        return original prompt tokens + generated tokens except the last one

    return original prompt tokens
```

Why exclude the last generated token? Your [DecodeBatch](./utils/batch.py) feeds that token on the *next* decode step. Including it in recompute would process it twice.

```text
prompt:            [A, B]
generated:         [X, Y]
recompute prefill: [A, B, X]
next decode:       [Y] → produce Z
```

Use `prefill_tokens(request)` wherever prefill currently reads `prompt_token_ids`: remaining-length calculations in the scheduler, token slicing in `PrefillBatch`, and the length checks in `advance_prefill()` and `complete_prefill()`.

### 2. Preempt one request

Add a request transition and an engine operation with roughly this logic:

```text
preempt(request):
    remember whether request is currently DECODING
    # If it is still in PREFILL, it has generated nothing yet.

    free request.block_table through the KV-cache manager
    remove request from scheduler.running

    request.num_computed_tokens = 0
    request.status = WAITING
    request.must_resume_decoding = whether it was DECODING

    append request to scheduler.waiting
```

Do **not** clear `generated_token_ids`, `emitted_text`, or `output_queue`. Do **not** send the stream-end marker or archive the request. A preempted request is still active.

Notice the two outcomes:

```text
Preempted during original PREFILL:
    rebuild original prompt
    sample its first generated token as usual

Preempted during DECODING:
    rebuild prompt + earlier generated tokens
    do not sample at the end of recompute
    decode the latest generated token on the next step
```

### 3. Retry scheduling after preemption

In [Engine.schedule_step()](./utils/engine.py:209), the current capacity check is where this begins:

```text
repeat:
    make a fresh scheduler plan
    calculate blocks needed by that plan

    if blocks_needed <= free_blocks:
        commit the plan
        return it

    choose a running victim that owns KV blocks

    if no suitable victim exists:
        raise KVCacheExhaustedError

    preempt the victim
    # The old plan is now invalid. Loop and make a NEW plan.
```

For the first version, choose the last running request with allocated blocks, but avoid preempting the **only** running request just to immediately readmit it. Bound the retries—at most one preemption per previously running request—so an impossible workload cannot loop forever.

Finally, in [Engine.process_prefill_batch()](./utils/engine.py:185), change what happens when the last recompute chunk finishes:

```text
if prefill is complete:
    remember whether this request must resume decoding
    change its status to DECODING

    if it must resume decoding:
        clear the resume flag
        do not sample, append, or stream a token
    else:
        sample and stream the first token normally
```

That “do not sample” branch is the most important correctness check. Without it, users would see an extra token after preemption.

> Still didnt understand

Let’s ignore the scheduler for a moment. Think of the KV cache as the model’s working notes. Preemption means **throw away one request’s notes, then recreate them later**. It does not mean restart the answer the user sees.

Suppose a request has:

```text
prompt_token_ids     = [10, 11]
generated_token_ids  = [50, 51]
num_computed_tokens  = 3
status               = DECODING
```

Its cache contains `[10, 11, 50]`. Token `51` is the next token your `DecodeBatch` will feed into the model.

Here is the entire pause-and-resume sequence:

| Moment | Cache contains | Generated tokens | Next action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Before preemption | `[10, 11, 50]` | `[50, 51]` | Decode `51` |
| After preemption | nothing | `[50, 51]` | Wait |
| After recompute | `[10, 11, 50]` again | `[50, 51]` | Decode `51` |
| After next decode | `[10, 11, 50, 51]` | `[50, 51, 52]` | Continue |

So the first piece to build is just this:

```text
pause request:
    free its KV blocks
    set num_computed_tokens to 0
    move it from running to waiting
    keep generated_token_ids unchanged
```

When it runs again, prefill `[10, 11, 50]` to restore the cache. **Do not sample a token from that prefill**—`51` was already generated and sent to the user. The next ordinary decode feeds `51` and produces `52`.

For a request paused *before* it generated anything, it’s simpler: prefill its original prompt again, then sample its first token normally.

That is why step 5 needs two pieces of state: “which tokens should I rebuild?” and “should I skip sampling when rebuilding finishes?” Get that request behavior working first; only then add the scheduler loop that chooses which request to pause.

Step 6 is fairness, but your [waiting queue](./utils/scheduler.py:21) already gives you one important guarantee: it is FIFO. New short requests join at the back, so they cannot repeatedly jump ahead of an older long request. I would **keep that order** for this version.

The fairness problem introduced by step 5 is different: [victim selection](./utils/engine.py:227) always chooses the last running request. A request that was just recomputed and admitted again could repeatedly lose its cache.

I suggest adding two counters to each `Request`:

```text
waiting_steps = 0
preemption_count = 0
```

Update them only when something actually happens:

```text
When a scheduler plan is committed:
    for each request still in waiting:
        waiting_steps += 1

When a request is preempted:
    preemption_count += 1
```

Do not increment `waiting_steps` inside `plan()`: step 5 can call `plan()` several times before committing one step, which would count retries as real waiting time.

Then choose a victim from running requests that own blocks:

```text
Prefer the request with:
    1. fewer previous preemptions
    2. less accumulated waiting time
    3. if still tied, the most recently admitted request
```

That keeps your current “last running request” behavior for ties, but protects a request after it has already paid the cost of recomputing. Keep the existing rule that the sole running request is not preempted just to readmit itself.

I would not sort the waiting queue by a score yet. Your [Scheduler.commit()](./utils/scheduler.py:65) assumes admissions come from the front of that queue; changing the selection order would require changing commit as well. FIFO admission plus fairer victim selection is a clean, testable step 6.

The issue is that your `.env` has `HF_TOKEN=...`, but not `export HF_TOKEN=...`. `source .env` creates a variable in your shell; without `export`, the Python process cannot see it. Hugging Face reads `HF_TOKEN` from the process environment. [Hugging Face documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/huggingface_hub/en/package_reference/environment_variables)

In the **same terminal** where you run Python:

```bash
source .env
export HF_TOKEN
python -c 'import os; print(bool(os.getenv("HF_TOKEN")))'
```

That check should print `True` without revealing the token. Then run your benchmark or tests from that terminal. Alternatively, change the line in `.env` to `export HF_TOKEN=...`. Your `.env` is already gitignored, and I made no changes.

Seventh version, step 1 is about deciding **which blocks are safe to reuse**. You do not need hashing or sharing yet; those are steps 2 and 3.

Your `Request.block_table` maps logical blocks to physical KV-cache blocks. A block becomes eligible only when all its positions contain **prompt tokens** and the model has finished writing its KV values for **every layer**.

For example, with `block_size = 4` and a 10-token prompt:

```text
block 0: prompt tokens 0–3   → complete
block 1: prompt tokens 4–7   → complete
block 2: prompt tokens 8–9   → partial; keep private
```

The code logic can be:

```text
After a prefill batch has successfully run:
    computed_prompt_tokens = min(request.num_computed_tokens, len(request.prompt_token_ids))
    complete_block_count = computed_prompt_tokens // block_size

    For each prompt block before complete_block_count:
        identify its physical ID from request.block_table
        mark it eligible for future prefix caching
```

Put the eligibility decision near the end of `Engine.process_prefill_batch()`, **after** `process_batch()` has returned and `advance_prefill()` has updated the count. Do not decide from `block_table` length alone: its final entry may be partial. Use `prompt_token_ids`, not `prefill_token_ids`, because the latter can also contain generated tokens when a preempted request resumes.

For this step, I would test prompts of 3, 4, 6 and 8 tokens with a block size of 4, including a prompt processed across multiple prefill chunks. The eligible block counts should be 0, 1, 1 and 2 respectively. Leave the `500 × 500` cache defaults as they are.

> How do I mark a prompt block eligible for future prefix caching?

For step 1, “mark eligible” can be a small piece of metadata in `PagedKVCache`: a set of physical block IDs, such as `cacheable_blocks`. It does **not** mean sharing the block yet.

```text
After process_batch() finishes and advance_prefill() updates the request:
    complete_prompt_blocks = min(num_computed_tokens, prompt_length) // block_size

    For each of those logical block positions:
        physical_id = request.block_table[logical_position]
        add physical_id to cacheable_blocks
```

Do this only after the model forward pass returns, so every layer has written its KV values. When a physical block is actually freed and returned to `free_blocks`, remove its ID from `cacheable_blocks`; that ID may later be allocated for unrelated tokens.

One useful distinction: the **request** tells you how many prompt blocks are complete; `PagedKVCache` owns the physical block ID and its metadata. In steps 2–3, you’ll associate those eligible blocks with hashes and make them reusable.

> Now step 2

Step 2 gives each complete prompt block a key that describes **both its tokens and everything before it**. You’re not reusing blocks yet; that is step 3.

Suppose `block_size = 4`:

```text
Prompt A: [10, 11, 12, 13] [20, 21, 22, 23]
Prompt B: [99, 11, 12, 13] [20, 21, 22, 23]
```

The second blocks have identical tokens, but their preceding context differs, so they must have different hashes. That is why each hash includes the previous block’s hash.

```text
parent_hash = a fixed starting value

For each complete prompt block, in order:
    block_tokens = prompt_token_ids[start : start + block_size]
    block_hash = stable_hash(parent_hash, block_tokens, model_identity, adapter_id)
    associate block_hash with this block's physical ID
    parent_hash = block_hash
```

In your project, I’d add a `block_hashes` dictionary to `PagedKVCache`, keyed by physical block ID. When [`Engine.process_prefill_batch()`](./utils/engine.py:186) discovers a newly complete block, it already has the logical position and physical ID; use the logical position to slice `request.prompt_token_ids`, then compute and record its hash. For its parent, use the hash of the preceding logical block, or the fixed starting value for block 0. Remove a block’s hash when its physical ID is freed, just as you do for `cacheable_blocks`.

Use a deterministic digest such as SHA-256, with an unambiguous encoding of the inputs. Don’t use `request_id`—two requests need to produce the same hash for the same prefix. You have no LoRA adapters yet, so use one fixed “no adapter” value; leave a place to incorporate an adapter ID later.

You have the right starting structure: `block_hashes` belongs with the physical blocks in `PagedKVCache`. The slice you’ve started in [`process_prefill_batch()`](./utils/engine.py:199) needs one correction: `prompt_token_ids[:logical_block * block_size]` gives you the *earlier* tokens, not the tokens in this block.

For each newly complete block, think:

```text
start = logical_block * block_size
tokens = prompt_token_ids[start : start + block_size]

if logical_block == 0:
    parent_hash = a fixed starting value
else:
    previous_physical_id = block_table[logical_block - 1]
    parent_hash = block_hashes[previous_physical_id]

digest = hash(parent_hash, tokens, model_identity, adapter_id)
block_hashes[physical_id] = digest
```

A straightforward SHA-256 helper uses JSON for unambiguous, repeatable input:

```python
import hashlib
import json

def hash_block(parent_hash, tokens, model_identity, adapter_id=None):
    payload = json.dumps(
        [parent_hash, tokens, model_identity, adapter_id],
        separators=(",", ":")
    ).encode("utf-8")
    return hashlib.sha256(payload).hexdigest()
```

Use the same fixed `parent_hash` for every first block. There is no adapter support yet, so `None` is fine. Since each `Engine` owns one model and one cache, a fixed model identity for that engine is sufficient for now; don’t include `request_id`.

Finally, remove `block_hashes[block_id]` when that block’s reference count reaches zero, alongside your `cacheable_blocks.discard(block_id)`. That prevents a reused physical ID from inheriting an old hash.

> | Continuing a bit the discussion we had offline for others to chime in.After quite some discussion and thinking, I see the following problem:- I don't want to clutter `generate()` with if-statements anymore as it's done a bit in this PR, but rather make use of tools like `LogitsProcessor`. Now @Narsil you gave me some very good arguments to why just adding a `LogitsProcessor` that forces to generate EOS is not good enough (Some models don't have the EOS token & we don't always want to have EOS at the end of the sentence). So I would propose the following solution that we should then also use to deprecate `max_length` from the "lower" generate methods like `greedy_search`, `sample`, ...Analogs to `LogitsProcessor` and `LogitsProcessorList`, we create a new logit called `StoppingCriteria` and `StoppingCriteriaList` which would look as follows:`<br>class StoppingCriteriaList(list):<br>    def __call__(self, input_ids: torch.LongTensor, scores: torch.FloatTensor, **kwargs) -> torch.FloatTensor:<br>        stopping = False<br>        for criteria in self:<br>           stopping = stopping or criteria(input_ids, scores)<br>        return stopping<br>`and a `MaxTimeStopping` class as follows:`<br>class MaxTimeStopping(StoppingCriteria):<br>    def __init__(self, max_time):<br>        self.start_time = time.time()<br>        self.max_time = max_time<br>    def __call__(self, *args):<br>        if time.time() - self.start_time > self.max_time:<br>            return True<br>       return False<br>`The same way we can create a `MaxLengthStopping` class as follows:`<br>class MaxLengthStopping(StoppingCriteria):<br>    def __init__(self, max_length):<br>        self.start_time = time.time()<br>        self.max_length = max_length<br>    def __call__(self, input_ids, *args):<br>       if input_ids.shape[-1] > self.max_length:<br>           return True<br>       return False<br>`Then we can add create a `stopping_criteria` list object in generate along side creating the `logits_processor` list object and pass it to the submodules. In each submodule we would then do something like`<br>if stopping_criteria(input_ids, scores):<br>    break;<br>`I would then also deprecate the `max_length` as an input parameter to `greedy_search` etc and add a `stopping_criteria` list object instead.This new approach would open the way for more fancy stopping criteria. E.g. at the moment `max_length` defines the number of total tokens (passed tokens + generated tokens) instead of just the generated tokens which is very hard to change in terms of backwards compatibility. Lots of people have complained about that. With this approach, one could easily make a new `MaxGeneratedTokenStopping` class that would then take over.Another positive effect of this function is that we can easily test & optimize those classes as we've already seen it for the `LogitsProcessor` classes.This will require a rather big change, so I'd be very glad if @LysandreJik and @sgugger you can give your opinion here before proceeding. |

I'm very down to continue the modular approach we have with processors, the new `StoppingCriteria` you propose seems like the way to go. It's good that it keeps the extensibility of the generation methods while not complexifying the generate method itself. |

>           "text": "# What does this PR do?\n## Who can review?\n|  |\n|-|\n| Continuing a bit the discussion we had offline for others to chime in.After quite some discussion and thinking, I see the following problem:- I don't want to clutter `generate()` with if-statements anymore as it's done a bit in this PR, but rather make use of tools like `LogitsProcessor`. Now @Narsil you gave me some very good arguments to why just adding a `LogitsProcessor` that forces to generate EOS is not good enough (Some models don't have the EOS token & we don't always want to have EOS at the end of the sentence). So I would propose the following solution that we should then also use to deprecate `max_length` from the \"lower\" generate methods like `greedy_search`, `sample`, ...Analogs to `LogitsProcessor` and `LogitsProcessorList`, we create a new logit called `StoppingCriteria` and `StoppingCriteriaList` which would look as follows:`<br>class StoppingCriteriaList(list):<br>    def __call__(self, input_ids: torch.LongTensor, scores: torch.FloatTensor, **kwargs) -> torch.FloatTensor:<br>        stopping = False<br>        for criteria in self:<br>           stopping = stopping or criteria(input_ids, scores)<br>        return stopping<br>`and a `MaxTimeStopping` class as follows:`<br>class MaxTimeStopping(StoppingCriteria):<br>    def __init__(self, max_time):<br>        self.start_time = time.time()<br>        self.max_time = max_time<br>    def __call__(self, *args):<br>        if time.time() - self.start_time > self.max_time:<br>            return True<br>       return False<br>`The same way we can create a `MaxLengthStopping` class as follows:`<br>class MaxLengthStopping(StoppingCriteria):<br>    def __init__(self, max_length):<br>        self.start_time = time.time()<br>        self.max_length = max_length<br>    def __call__(self, input_ids, *args):<br>       if input_ids.shape[-1] > self.max_length:<br>           return True<br>       return False<br>`Then we can add create a `stopping_criteria` list object in generate along side creating the `logits_processor` list object and pass it to the submodules. In each submodule we would then do something like`<br>if stopping_criteria(input_ids, scores):<br>    break;<br>`I would then also deprecate the `max_length` as an input parameter to `greedy_search` etc and add a `stopping_criteria` list object instead.This new approach would open the way for more fancy stopping criteria. E.g. at the moment `max_length` defines the number of total tokens (passed tokens + generated tokens) instead of just the generated tokens which is very hard to change in terms of backwards compatibility. Lots of people have complained about that. With this approach, one could easily make a new `MaxGeneratedTokenStopping` class that would then take over.Another positive effect of this function is that we can easily test & optimize those classes as we've already seen it for the `LogitsProcessor` classes.This will require a rather big change, so I'd be very glad if @LysandreJik and @sgugger you can give your opinion here before proceeding. |\n\n|  |\n|-|\n| Thanks for the thoughtful explanation, this makes a lot of sense. I'm very down to continue the modular approach we have with processors, the new `StoppingCriteria` you propose seems like the way to go. It's good that it keeps the extensibility of the generation methods while not complexifying the generate method itself. |\n\nComment threadsrc/transformers/generation_stopping_criteria.py\n\nand remove this statement in the `generate()` method?\n\n[https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/master/src/transformers/generation\\_utils.py#L1418](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/master/src/transformers/generation\\_utils.py#L1418)\n\nComment threadsrc/transformers/generation_stopping_criteria.py\n\n|  |  |  |\n|-|-|-|\n|  |  | break |\n|  |  |  |\n|  |  | if stopping_criteria(input_ids, scores): |"
