I ran both benchmarks on your Mac’s **MPS GPU** with the exact prompt. Both produced identical response text.

| 32-token run | Hugging Face | Custom engine |
|---|---:|---:|
| Eager generation | 2.85 s | 3.28 s |
| Eager decode | 11.28 tok/s | 9.97 tok/s |
| SDPA-run generation | 2.82 s | 3.09 s |
| SDPA-run decode | 11.47 tok/s | 10.54 tok/s |

The custom engine is still slower. SDPA narrowed the gap in this single run, but **its decode path is unchanged**, so this is not evidence that SDPA sped up decode.

I also completed a short MPS profile using the same prompt and 4 generated tokens. Its CPU-side table showed 1,553 `copy_` calls taking 381 ms of 488 ms self CPU time; scheduling took 11.5 ms. That points toward copy/conversion overhead as the next thing to investigate, though the CPU table alone does not establish GPU kernel time. MPS memory was about 6.6 GiB. The initial 32-token profile was stopped during its unusually long warm-up.

Model loading was highly variable—216–253 s for the custom model in these runs—and is separate from the generation figures. I made no code changes during these measurements.

> ## [web:https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/faster-attenion-with-mps-backend/224884] (web) Faster Attenion with MPS backend - PyTorch Forums
> It wraps Apple's scaledDotProductAttention MPS Graph operation which frequently out-performs PyTorch's scaled_dot_product_attention with the MPS

> ## [doc:https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/8cfd4c5abdc325b07b526f0b27f78c469c0b7a5f/docs/source/en/model_doc/deit.md] (doc) DeiT
> ### Using Scaled Dot Product Attention (SDPA)
>
> PyTorch includes a native scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) operator as part of `torch.nn.functional`. This function
> encompasses several implementations that can be applied depending on the inputs and the hardware in use. See the
> official documentation
> or the GPU Inference
> page for more information.
>
> SDPA is used by default for `torch>=2.1.1` when an implementation is available, but you may also set
> `attn_implementation="sdpa"` in `from_pretrained()` to explicitly request SDPA to be used.
>
> ```python
> from transformers import DeiTForImageClassification
>
> model = DeiTForImageClassification.from_pretrained("facebook/deit-base-distilled-patch16-224", attn_implementation="sdpa", device_map="auto")
> ...
> ```
>
> For the best speedups, we recommend loading the model in half-precision (e.g. `torch.float16` or `torch.bfloat16`).
>
> On a local benchmark (A100-40GB, PyTorch 2.3.0, OS Ubuntu 22.04) with `float32` and `facebook/deit-base-distilled-patch16-224` model, we saw the following speedups during inference.
>
> |   Batch size |   Average inference time (ms), eager mode |   Average inference time (ms), sdpa model |   Speed up, Sdpa / Eager (x) |
> |--------------|-------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|------------------------------|
> |            1 |                                         8 |                                         6 |                      1.33 |
> |            2 |                                         9 |                                         6 |                      1.5  |
> |            4 |                                         9 |                                         6 |                      1.5  |
> |            8 |                                         8 |                                         6 |                      1.33 |
>
> ## [doc:https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/8cfd4c5abdc325b07b526f0b27f78c469c0b7a5f/docs/source/en/model_doc/videomae.md] (doc) VideoMAE
> ## Using Scaled Dot Product Attention (SDPA)
>
> PyTorch includes a native scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) operator as part of `torch.nn.functional`. This function
> encompasses several implementations that can be applied depending on the inputs and the hardware in use. See the
> official documentation
> or the GPU Inference
> page for more information.
>
> SDPA is used by default for `torch>=2.1.1` when an implementation is available, but you may also set
> `attn_implementation="sdpa"` in `from_pretrained()` to explicitly request SDPA to be used.
>
> ```python
> from transformers import VideoMAEForVideoClassification
>
> model = VideoMAEForVideoClassification.from_pretrained("MCG-NJU/videomae-base-finetuned-kinetics", attn_implementation="sdpa", device_map="auto")
> ...
> ```
>
> For the best speedups, we recommend loading the model in half-precision (e.g. `torch.float16` or `torch.bfloat16`).
>
> On a local benchmark (A100-40GB, PyTorch 2.3.0, OS Ubuntu 22.04) with `float32` and `MCG-NJU/videomae-base-finetuned-kinetics` model, we saw the following speedups during inference.
>
> |   Batch size |   Average inference time (ms), eager mode |   Average inference time (ms), sdpa model |   Speed up, Sdpa / Eager (x) |
> |--------------|-------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|------------------------------|
> |            1 |                                        37 |                                        10 |                      3.7  |
> |            2 |                                        24 |                                        18 |                      1.33 |
> |            4 |                                        43 |                                        32 |                      1.34 |
> |            8 |                                        84 |                                        60 |                      1.4  |
>

> https://github.com/tashiscool/fp8-mps-metal
> # fp8-mps-metal
> This repo contains a Metal compute shader that performs FP8 (e4m3fn) dequantization and matrix multiplication directly on the GPU, exposed to PyTorch as a drop-in monkey-patch.
>
> ## Quick Start
>
> The Metal shader compiles at runtime via `torch.mps.compile_shader()`.
>
> ## [doc:https://github.com/deepspeedai/deepspeed/blob/dc046b15d7a58f6c8dacba435508b52b1ebc620c/docs/_tutorials/accelerator-setup-guide.md] (doc) DeepSpeed Accelerator Setup Guides
> ## How to use DeepSpeed on Apple Silicon
>
> Launch a single-process job as usual; no hostfile is needed:
>
> ```
> deepspeed --num_gpus 1 train.py --deepspeed --deepspeed_config ds_config.json
> ```
>
> ZeRO stages 0 through 3 are supported with fp32, fp16, and bf16 (bf16 requires macOS 14 or newer), with or without ZeRO-Offload.
>
> The fused Adam optimizer is a Metal kernel compiled at first use through `torch.mps.compile_shader`; no Xcode project or C++ build is involved. ZeRO-Offload uses the C++ `DeepSpeedCPUAdam` kernel, which is built just-in-time with the system clang. Apple's clang has no OpenMP, so the kernel is single-threaded unless Homebrew's `libomp` is installed (`brew install libomp`), in which case it is picked up automatically. On unified memory, offload does not increase total memory - CPU and GPU share the same DRAM - so it is not needed for capacity the way it is on discrete GPUs. It still helps when the GPU working-set budget binds (Metal caps a process's GPU working set below total RAM): optimizer states held as CPU tensors stay outside that budget, and the optimizer step runs on the CPU cores.
>
> ## Limitations
>
> * PyTorch exposes one MPS device per machine, so `device_count()` is 1 and multi-device data parallelism on a single Mac is not possible.
> * There is no native collective backend for MPS. DeepSpeed uses `gloo` and stages tensors through CPU memory for each collective. This is cheap on unified memory, but multi-machine training over gloo is untested.
> * MPS does not support fp64; gradient norms are accumulated in fp32 on this backend.
> * MPS has no user-visible streams, so DeepSpeed treats it as a synchronized device and does not overlap communication with computation.
> * Tests and multiprocessing code must use the `spawn` start method, because MPS cannot be used from a forked child process.
> ````

> ## [doc:https://github.com/huggingface/blog/blob/2f4b37565a638ca5ad98a0ef8d8aea7a90f907bd/mps-pytorch-2-15.md] (doc) MPS in PyTorch 2.15
> ## What this means for you
>
> If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:
>
> - **Much faster local LLMs.** Mixture-of-experts models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: on an M3 Ultra with `torch.compile`, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s and LFM2.5-8B-A1B from 23.6 to 123.6 tokens/s. Dense models benefit too, from faster linear layers and an 8× faster softmax for sampling. (More)
> - **Video generation that fits in memory.** Decoding a video with Wan2.2's tiled VAE used to push driver memory to 270 GiB; it now peaks at about 8 GiB. (More)
> - **Correct image editing with Qwen-Image-2.1.** On 2.14, the Qwen-Image-2.1 VAE encoder silently corrupted images on MPS, breaking image-edit workflows (reported in ComfyUI). The same padding change fixes it: an encode-decode round trip now matches CPU at 29.95 dB PSNR, up from 10.06 dB.
> - **FP8 weights on your Mac.** FP8 tensors take half the memory of BF16, and `F.scaled_mm` multiplies them directly on the GPU. (More)
>
> ## Contents
>
> - Getting started
> - FP8 comes to MPS
> - Faster language-model decoding
> - Linear algebra gets a boost
> - Convolutions, padding, and training
> - Softmax and reductions
> - A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding
> - More control with MPS streams
> - More operations work on MPS
> - A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16
> - Wrapping up
>
> ## Getting started
>
> You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with **macOS 15 or later** and **Python 3.11 or later** (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.
>
> To try the release candidate in a separate environment:
>
> ```bash
> uv pip install torch==2.15.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/test/cpu
> ```
>
> ## [doc:https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/8cfd4c5abdc325b07b526f0b27f78c469c0b7a5f/docs/source/en/apple_silicon.md] (doc) Apple Silicon
> # Apple Silicon
> Apple Silicon (M-series) chips run PyTorch through the Metal Performance Shaders (MPS) backend, with the device string `mps`.
>
> MPS works with the standard `torch` install. Check that PyTorch was built with MPS and can see the GPU.
>
> It prints `True` when MPS is ready to use.
>

>

> - Read the PyTorch MPS backend notes for supported operations and known issues.

For your Mac, I’d adjust the remaining version 8 steps around the measured bottleneck. The profile showed **1,553 `copy_` calls in four steps**; that makes copy/conversion overhead worth investigating, but the CPU-side table does not yet prove where GPU time is spent.

1. **Make the comparison repeatable.** Load each model once, warm it up, then run several fresh requests with the same prompt. Compare generated token IDs and median TTFT/decode speed. Our one-run SDPA difference is too small to trust yet.
2. **Locate the copies.** Profile `RMSNorm`, `PagedKVCache.append()`, and `direct_paged_read()` separately. Check which casts or per-token writes account for the `copy_` calls.
3. **A/B test MPS decode attention.** Compare the current per-block read with a gather-plus-SDPA path on the *same loaded model*. Keep the faster path only if cached outputs and generated token IDs still match.
4. **Fuse only the confirmed hot operation.** On MPS, the custom-kernel route is a Metal shader via [`torch.mps.compile_shader`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.mps.compile_shader.html), not Triton. Start with one small kernel and a parity test.
5. **Then revisit quantization and loading.** Your 216–253 s custom load times need a separate investigation; they are not included in generation throughput.

I would defer the document’s CUDA Graph step—it is not an MPS step—and leave multi-GPU for a different machine. After the engine’s token parity and MPS speed are stable, the HTTP server and metrics are the next independent milestone.

> `torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention` is usable with any architecture that uses standard attention, and namely replaces the boiler-plate code:

> ```py
> # native scaled_dot_product_attention is equivalent to the following:

> 	scale_factor = 1 / math.sqrt(Q.size(-1)) if scale is None else scale
> 	attn_mask = torch.ones(L, S, dtype=torch.bool).tril(diagonal=0) if is_causal else attn_mask
> 	attn_mask = attn_mask.masked_fill(not attn_mask, -float('inf')) if attn_mask.dtype==torch.bool else attn_mask
> 	attn_weight = torch.softmax((Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) * scale_factor) + attn_mask, dim=-1)
> 	attn_weight = torch.dropout(attn_weight, dropout_p)
> 	return attn_weight @ V
> ```

> In the 🤗 Optimum integration with Transformers models, the following architectures are supported for now: gpt2, gpt-neo, gpt-neox, gptj, t5, bart, codegen, pegasus, opt, LLaMA, blenderbot, m2m100. You can expect this list to be extended in the near future!
>
> To validate the benefits from the native scaled dot-product attention, we ran inference and training benchmarks, whose results are presented below.
>
> Inference benchmark on a single A10G GPU, AWS g5.4xlarge instance_Inference benchmark on a single A10G GPU, AWS g5.4xlarge instance_
>

>
> Out of this benchmark, the most interesting finding is that native SDPA allows for the usage of longer sequence lengths and batch sizes without running into out of memory issues. Moreover, up to 20% speedups can be seen during inference, and even larger during training.
>
> As seen on the training benchmarks, it appears that smaller head dimension brings higher speedups and memory savings, which we will discuss in the following section.
>
> The implementation supports multi-GPU settings as well, thanks to 🤗 Accelerate library by passing `device_map=”auto”` to the `from_pretrained` method. Here are some results for training on two A100-SXM4-80GB.
>
> Training benchmark on two A100-SXM4-80GB, Nvidia DGX, using 🤗 Accelerate library for distributed training_Training benchmark on two A100-SXM4-80GB, Nvidia DGX, using 🤗 Accelerate library for distributed training_

> Note that some kernels support only the sm\_80 compute capability (which is the one from A100 GPUs), which limits usability on a wide range of hardware, notably if the head dimension is not a power of two. For example, as of PyTorch 2.0.0 during training, opt-2.7b (headim=80) and gpt-neox-20b (headdim=96) can not dispatch to a kernel using flash attention, unless run on an A100 GPU. Better kernels may be developed in the future: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/98140#issuecomment-1518101895

> ## [web:https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html] (web) torch.nn.functional. - PyTorch documentation
> Computes scaled dot product attention on query, key and value tensors, using an optional attention mask if passed, and applying dropout if a probability greater
>
> ## [doc:https://github.com/ascend/pytorch/blob/b90b272bbb5977bffa210c4730315a30882ccf88/docs/en/api/native_api/pytorch_2-14-0/torch-nn-functional.md] (doc) torch.nn.functional
> # torch.nn.functional
> ## Attention Mechanisms
> ### torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention
> - `query`, `key`, and `value` only support bf16, fp16, and fp32. All parameter inputs must comply with the following constraints:
> - All parameter inputs must comply with the specifications:
>   - N of input `query`, `key`, and `value`: batch size. Currently, only the layout [N, head_num, S(L), E(Ev)] is supported, with a value range of 1 to 2K.
>   - S of input `key` and `value`: Source sequence length, with a value range of 1 to 512K.
>   - E of input `query`, `key`, and `value`: Embedding dimension of the query and key, with a value range of 1 to 512.
>   - Input `attn_mask`: currently supports [N, 1, L, S], [N, head_num, L, S], [1, 1, L, S], [L, S], and bool-type masks that can be broadcast to [N, head_num, L, S], for example, layouts such as [L, 1], [1, S], and [1, 1].
>   - The data types of input `query`, `key`, and `value` are bf16, fp16, and fp32.
>
> ## [web:https://docs.pytorch.ac.cn/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html] (web) scaled_dot_product_attention - torch.nn.functional - PyTorch 文档
> 对query、key 和value 张量计算缩放点积注意力（scaled dot product attention），如果传入了可选的注意力掩码（attention mask）则会使用它，并且在指定的概率大于0.0 时

I implemented and committed the MPS performance work through `v8.8`. The worktree is clean.

The repeatable benchmark now checks greedy token IDs and reports three-run medians. On your Mac, gather-plus-SDPA decode measured **11.27 tokens/s** versus **9.93** for direct paged reads, with matching Hugging Face token IDs, so it is now the MPS default. A later run measured **11.63 tokens/s** for the custom engine versus **10.99** for Hugging Face; across runs, I’d call their decode performance roughly matched, not consistently faster.

I also changed the loader to assign checkpoint weights into a meta-device model, following [PyTorch’s loading recipe](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/recipes/recipes/module_load_state_dict_tips.html). Custom load time fell from **216–253 s** in the earlier runs to **57.54 s** in the measured follow-up. The full suite passes: **224 passed, 1 MPS-only test skipped in the sandbox**; that MPS test passed separately on your GPU.

I did **not** add a Metal kernel or quantization. The latest profiler run was severely distorted—about 89 s of reported copy time for generation that normally takes about 3 s—so it does not identify a trustworthy kernel target. Quantization still needs a separate accuracy and memory benchmark.

> ## [doc:https://pytorch.org/blog/pytorch-2-13-release-blog/] (doc) PyTorch 2.13 Release Blog
> ### **FlexAttention on Apple Silicon (MPS)**
>
> FlexAttention, PyTorch’s unified API for expressing custom attention patterns as plain Python functions compiled into fused kernels, is now available on Metal/MPS. The MPS implementation provides hand-written Metal kernels for both the sparse prefill and decode paths (including GQA and captured buffers). So instead of writing a custom CUDA kernel for every attention variant you need, FlexAttention will write a 2-line Python function, and the compiler builds a fast kernel for you automatically.
>
> The benchmark numbers are impressive for sparse masks. On long, sparse attention patterns the speedups over SDPA are substantial — e.g. on a 1×8×32768×64 shape with a 256-element sliding window (0.8% density), FlexAttention runs in ~35 ms vs ~431 ms for SDPA ( **~12.3x**); a smaller 8192-length / 64-window case achieves **~4.15x**. Dense patterns continue to favor SDPA, as expected. API Unstable
>
> (PR #182552, #186215, and #181575 by Irakli Salia, EPAM)
>
> ## **Core Features**
>
> ### **nn.LinearCrossEntropyLoss**
>
> In standard large-vocabulary training (e.g., language models with 100K+ token vocabularies), computing the cross-entropy loss requires materializing the entire logits matrix over the vocabulary, which can consume tens of gigabytes of GPU memory. nn.LinearCrossEntropyLoss (and the corresponding linear\_cross\_entropy functional) fuses the final linear projection and cross-entropy computation into a single module that processes the vocabulary dimension in chunks, never materializing the full logits matrix. This reduces peak memory by up to ~4x for large-vocabulary workloads while maintaining numerical equivalence with the unfused path. The implementation supports label smoothing, weight tying, and z-loss regularization out of the box, and integrates with torch.compile for further optimization. As a drop-in replacement for separate nn.Linear + nn.CrossEntropyLoss, adoption requires no other code changes.
>
> API Unstable
>
> (See #172446, #172286, and #185852 by Pearu Peterson, OpenTeams.)
>

> ## [pull_request:pytorch/executorch#19145] (pull_request) pytorch/executorch#19145
> https://github.com/pytorch/executorch/issues/19145
> ## Pull request overview
> Adds a new v2 entry point for the Metal/MPS scaled dot-product-attention (SDPA) fallback kernel to match an updated ABI that includes `enable_gqa`, while keeping the original v1 symbol for older `.pte` artifacts.
>
> ### Reviewed changes
> | File | Description |
> |-|-|
> | backends/apple/metal/runtime/ops/op_sdpa.mm | Adds v2 C entry point with `enable_gqa` and factors logic into a shared implementation. |
> | backends/apple/metal/metal_backend.py | Adds the v2 SDPA op overload name to the supported fallback kernels list. |
>
> `enable_gqa` is introduced in the shared implementation signature but never used. Since the Metal kernel uses `gqa_factor` to compute `kv_head_idx` (division), it would be safer to use `enable_gqa` to (a) validate head-count relationships (e.g., require Q heads == KV heads when disabled; require divisibility and Q heads >= KV heads when enabled) and (b) compute the correct `gqa_factor`. If the parameter is intentionally ignored because the kernel always supports GQA, please explicitly mark it unused and document that behavior to avoid silent mismatches.
>
> |  |  |  |
> |-|-|-|
> |  |  |  |
>
> |  |  |  |
> |-|-|-|
> |  |  | // v2: New signature with enable_gqa (for new .pte files). |
> |  |  | AOTITorchError aoti_torch_mps__scaled_dot_product_attention_math_for_mps_v2( |
> |  |  | AOTITensorHandle value, |
> |  |  | double* scale, |
> |  |  | int32_t enable_gqa, |
> |  |  | dropout_mask, scale, enable_gqa, ret0, ret1); |
> |  |  | } |
>
> This PR adds a v2 SDPA entry point to match the new `enable_gqa`-extended ABI, but the Metal backend test suite currently has SDPA coverage without exercising `enable_gqa`. Please add a Metal test module that calls `torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(..., enable_gqa=True)` (ideally with Q heads !

> I would also really appreciate GQA support for MPS. Is this a driver/feature limitation with Apple's MPS internal matmul/attention kernels?
>
> ## [issue:pytorch/pytorch#154363] (issue) `scaled_dot_product_attention` broadcasting (GQA) is a memory footgun#154363
> https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/154363
> # `scaled_dot_product_attention` broadcasting (GQA) is a memory footgun#154363
> ## Description
> ### 🐛 Describe the bug
> When investigating, I found `enable_gqa=True` (which to my understanding of #139586 requires cuDNN backend) but I don't understand its purpose.
>
> If it is about the implicit interleave, why is it only compatible with certain backends? If it uses a separate kernel, why can't it fall back to implicit interleave for remaining backends? I would argue that for the case where one of the head dimensions is 1 (broadcasting), PyTorch should select an efficient kernel (if available) regardless of `enable_gqa`.
>
> ### Versions
> Vulnerability Itlb multihit: Not affected
>
> Vulnerability Meltdown: Not affected
>
> Vulnerability Mmio stale data: Not affected
>
> Vulnerability Srbds: Not affected
>
> [conda] Could not collect
>
> The memory-efficient kernel does not support GQA in general, and the SDPA backend selection logic reflects this:
>
> 1. **Cheap:** make the silent MATH fallback noisy. A `UserWarning` at dispatch time when `enable_gqa=True` lands on MATH purely because no fused backend accepts the config would have saved this round-trip. Today users only see the relevant warnings if they explicitly force a non-MATH backend; the default path is silent.
>
> It only adds the cheap option (1) from my comment above: a `TORCH_WARN_ONCE` when `enable_gqa=True` is silently dispatched to MATH because no fused backend accepted the config. It does **not** attempt the larger kernel-side fix (adding GQA support to `mem_efficient`/cuDNN).
>
> ## [pull_request:nari-labs/dia#198] (pull_request) nari-labs/dia#198
> https://github.com/nari-labs/dia/issues/198
> ## Changes
> - **Why This Change?**: MPS has stricter tensor shape requirements than CUDA or CPU. The custom function avoids broadcasting issues that triggered `mps_matmul` errors, while preserving GQA functionality.
> ```

> ## [pull_request:pytorch/pytorch#100635] (pull_request) pytorch/pytorch#100635
> https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/100635
> - Enable event and interval-based os signpost tracing via env-var 'PYTORCH\_MPS\_TRACE\_SIGNPOSTS' (python bindings sent in separate PR).
> - Enable logging of MPS graphs, native kernels, and copies and their GPU times via env-var `PYTORCH_MPS_LOG_PROFILE_INFO`.
> - Enable dumping the table of kernel profiling results sorted based on Mean GPU time when the process ends (SIGINT also handled).
> - Fix a bug in MPSAllocator where the Allocator completionHandlers were called after MPSAllocator instance was destroyed.
> - Added option to use Schedule Handlers to begin signpost intervals.
> - Refer to comments in `MPSProfiler.h` to learn how to set env-vars for logging and signpost tracing. Proper documentation will be sent in a separate PR later.
>
>           [MPS] Add support for MPSProfiler
>
> ```
> - Enable event and interval-based os signpost tracing
> - Enable logging of MPS graphs, native kernels, and copies and their GPU times
> - Enable dumping the table of kernel profiling results sorted
>   based on Mean GPU time when the process ends.
> - Fix a bug in MPSAllocator where the Allocator completionHandlers were called
>   after MPSAllocator instance was destroyed.
> - Use Schedule Handlers to begin signpost intervals. (can be disabled via flag INCLUDE_SCHEDULE_INTERVAL).
> * Only dump Copy Stats which have copies logged
> ```

torch.nn.functional.scaled\\_dot\\_product\\_attention [\\#](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html\\#torch-nn-functional-scaled-dot-product-attention \"Link to this heading\")\n\ntorch.nn.functional.scaled\\_dot\\_product\\_attention() [\\[source\\]](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v2.14.0/torch/nn/functional.py#L6367) [#](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html#torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention \"Link to this definition\")scaled\\_dot\\_product\\_attention(query, key, value, attn\\_mask=None, dropout\\_p=0.0,\n\nis\\_causal=False, scale=None, enable\\_gqa=False) -> Tensor:\n\nComputes scaled dot product attention on query, key and value tensors, using an optional attention mask if passed,\nand applying dropout if a probability greater than 0.0 is specified. The optional scale argument can only be\nspecified as a keyword argument.\n\n```\n# Efficient implementation equivalent to the following:\ndef scaled_dot_product_attention(query, key, value, attn_mask=None, dropout_p=0.0,\n        is_causal=False, scale=None, enable_gqa=False) -> torch.Tensor:\n    L, S = query.size(-2), key.size(-2)\n    scale_factor = 1 / math.sqrt(query.size(-1)) if scale is None else scale\n    attn_bias = torch.zeros(L, S, dtype=query.dtype, device=query.device)\n    if is_causal:\n        assert attn_mask is None\n        temp_mask = torch.ones(L, S, dtype=torch.bool, device=query.device).tril(diagonal=0)\n        attn_bias.masked_fill_(temp_mask.logical_not(), float(\"-inf\"))\n\n    if attn_mask is not None:\n        if attn_mask.dtype == torch.bool:\n            attn_bias.masked_fill_(attn_mask.logical_not(), float(\"-inf\"))\n        else:\n            attn_bias = attn_mask + attn_bias\n\n    if enable_gqa:\n        key = key.repeat_interleave(query.size(-3)//key.size(-3), -3)\n        value = value.repeat_interleave(query.size(-3)//value.size(-3), -3)\n\n    attn_weight = query @ key.transpose(-2, -1) * scale_factor\n    attn_weight += attn_bias\n    attn_weight = torch.softmax(attn_weight, dim=-1)\n    attn_weight = torch.dropout(attn_weight, dropout_p, train=True)\n    return attn_weight @ value\n```\n\nCopy to clipboard\n\nWarning\n\nThis function is beta and subject to change.\n\nWarning\n\nThis function always applies dropout according to the specified `dropout_p` argument.\nTo disable dropout during evaluation, be sure to pass a value of `0.0` when the module\nthat makes the function call is not in training mode.\n\nFor example:\n\n```\nclass MyModel(nn.Module):\n    def __init__(self, p=0.5):\n        super().__init__()\n        self.p = p\n\n    def forward(self, ...):\n        return F.scaled_dot_product_attention(...,\n            dropout_p=(self.p if self.training else 0.0))\n```\n\nCopy to clipboard\n\nNote\n\nThe boolean mask semantics for `attn_mask` are the inverse of\n[`MultiheadAttention`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.MultiheadAttention.html#torch.nn.MultiheadAttention \"torch.nn.MultiheadAttention\")’s `key_padding_mask`.\n\nIn [`scaled_dot_product_attention()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html#torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention \"torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention\"), `True` indicates values\nto **participate** in attention.\n\nIn [`MultiheadAttention`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.MultiheadAttention.html#torch.nn.MultiheadAttention \"torch.nn.MultiheadAttention\"), `True` indicates values\nto be **masked out** (padding).\n\nIf migrating from MHA, ensure you invert your boolean mask (e.g.,\nusing `~mask` or `mask.logical_not()`).\n\nNote\n\nThere are currently three supported implementations of scaled dot product attention:\n\n> - [FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08691)\n>\n> - [Memory-Efficient Attention](https://github.com/facebookresearch/xformers)\n>\n> - A PyTorch implementation defined in C++ matching the above formulation\n\nThe function may call optimized kernels for improved performance when using the CUDA backend.\nFor all other backends, the PyTorch implementation will be used.\n\nAll implementations are enabled by default. Scaled dot product attention attempts to automatically select the\nmost optimal implementation based on the inputs. In order to provide more fine-grained control over what implementation\nis used, the following functions are provided for enabling and disabling implementations.\nThe context manager is the preferred mechanism:\n\n> - [`torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel.html#torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel \"torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel\"): A context manager used to enable or disable any of the implementations.\n>\n> - [`torch.backends.cuda.enable_flash_sdp()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/backends.html#torch.backends.cuda.enable_flash_sdp \"torch.backends.cuda.enable_flash_sdp\"): Globally enables or disables FlashAttention.\n>\n> - [`torch.backends.cuda.enable_mem_efficient_sdp()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/backends.html#torch.backends.cuda.enable_mem_efficient_sdp \"torch.backends.cuda.enable_mem_efficient_sdp\"): Globally enables or disables Memory-Efficient Attention.\n>\n> - [`torch.backends.cuda.enable_math_sdp()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/backends.html#torch.backends.cuda.enable_math_sdp \"torch.backends.cuda.enable_math_sdp\"): Globally enables or disables the PyTorch C++ implementation.\n\nEach of the fused kernels has specific input limitations. If the user requires the use of a specific fused implementation,\ndisable the PyTorch C++ implementation using [`torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel.html#torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel \"torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel\").\nIn the event that a fused implementation is not available, a warning will be raised with the\nreasons why the fused implementation cannot run.\n\nDue to the nature of fusing floating point operations, the output of this function may be different\ndepending on what backend kernel is chosen.\nThe c++ implementation supports torch.float64 and can be used when higher precision is required.\nFor math backend, all intermediates are kept in torch.float if inputs are in torch.half or torch.bfloat16.\n\nFor more information please see [Numerical accuracy](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/numerical_accuracy.html)\n\n> Grouped Query Attention (GQA) is an experimental feature. It works with FlashAttention,\n> cuDNN attention, and the math kernel on CUDA tensors. Memory-efficient attention also supports\n> GQA on NVIDIA CUDA. GQA does not support Nested tensors.\n> Constraints for GQA:\n>\n> > - number\\_of\\_heads\\_query % number\\_of\\_heads\\_key\\_value == 0 and,\n> >\n> > - number\\_of\\_heads\\_key == number\\_of\\_heads\\_value\n\nNote\n\nIn some circumstances when given tensors on a CUDA device and using CuDNN, this operator may select a nondeterministic algorithm to increase performance. If this is undesirable, you can try to make the operation deterministic (potentially at a performance cost) by setting `torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True`. See [Reproducibility](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/randomness.html) for more information.\n\nParameters:\n\n- **query** ( [_Tensor_](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/tensors.html#torch.Tensor \"torch.Tensor\")) – Query tensor; shape (N,...,Hq,L,E)(N, ..., Hq, L, E)(N,...,Hq,L,E).\n\n- **key** ( [_Tensor_](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/tensors.html#torch.Tensor \"torch.Tensor\")) – Key tensor; shape (N,...,H,S,E)(N, ..., H, S, E)(N,...,H,S,E).\n\n- **value** ( [_Tensor_](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/tensors.html#torch.Tensor \"torch.Tensor\")) – Value tensor; shape (N,...,H,S,Ev)(N, ..., H, S, Ev)(N,...,H,S,Ev).\n\n- **attn\\_mask** ( _optional Tensor_) – Attention mask; shape must be broadcastable to the shape of attention weights,\nwhich is (N,...,Hq,L,S)(N,..., Hq, L, S)(N,...,Hq,L,S). Two types of masks are supported.\nA boolean mask where a value of True indicates that the element _should_ take part in attention.\nA float mask of the same type as query, key, value that is added to the attention score.\n\n- **dropout\\_p** ( [_float_](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#float \"(in Python v3.14)\")) – Dropout probability; if greater than 0.0, dropout is applied\n\n- **is\\_causal** ( [_bool_](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#bool \"(in Python v3.14)\")) – If set to true, the attention masking is a lower triangular matrix when the mask is a\nsquare matrix. The attention masking has the form of the upper left causal bias due to the alignment\n(see [`torch.nn.attention.bias.CausalBias`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.attention.bias.CausalBias.html#torch.nn.attention.bias.CausalBias \"torch.nn.attention.bias.CausalBias\")) when the mask is a non-square matrix.\nAn error is thrown if both attn\\_mask and is\\_causal are set.\n\n- **scale** ( _optional python:float_ _,_ _keyword-only_) – Scaling factor applied prior to softmax. If None, the default value is set\nto 1E\\\\frac{1}{\\\\sqrt{E}}E​1​.\n\n- **enable\\_gqa** ( [_bool_](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#bool \"(in Python v3.14)\")) – If set to True, Grouped Query Attention (GQA) is enabled, by default it is set to False.\n\n\nReturns:\n\nAttention output; shape (N,...,Hq,L,Ev)(N, ..., Hq, L, Ev)(N,...,Hq,L,Ev).\n\nReturn type:\n\noutput ( [Tensor](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/tensors.html#torch.Tensor \"torch.Tensor\"))\n\nShape legend:\n\n- N:Batch size...:Any number of other batch dimensions (optional)N: \\\\text{Batch size} ... : \\\\text{Any number of other batch dimensions (optional)}N:Batch size...:Any number of other batch dimensions (optional)\n\n- S:Source sequence lengthS: \\\\text{Source sequence length}S:Source sequence length\n\n- L:Target sequence lengthL: \\\\text{Target sequence length}L:Target sequence length\n\n- E:Embedding dimension of the query and keyE: \\\\text{Embedding dimension of the query and key}E:Embedding dimension of the query and key\n\n- Ev:Embedding dimension of the valueEv: \\\\text{Embedding dimension of the value}Ev:Embedding dimension of the value\n\n- Hq:Number of heads of queryHq: \\\\text{Number of heads of query}Hq:Number of heads of query\n\n- H:Number of heads of key and valueH: \\\\text{Number of heads of key and value}H:Number of heads of key and value\n\n\nExamples\n\n```\n>>> # Optionally use the context manager to ensure one of the fused kernels is run\n>>> query = torch.rand(32, 8, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> key = torch.rand(32, 8, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> value = torch.rand(32, 8, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> with sdpa_kernel(backends=[SDPBackend.FLASH_ATTENTION]):\n>>>     F.scaled_dot_product_attention(query,key,value)\n```\n\nCopy to clipboard\n\n```\n>>> # Sample for GQA for llama3\n>>> query = torch.rand(32, 32, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> key = torch.rand(32, 8, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> value = torch.rand(32, 8, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> with sdpa_kernel(backends=[SDPBackend.MATH]):\n>>>     F.scaled_dot_product_attention(query,key,value,enable_gqa=True)\n```\n\nCopy to clipboard\n\nOn this page\n\n\n[Show Source](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/_sources/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.rst.txt)\n\nPyTorch Libraries\n\n- [ExecuTorch](https://docs.pytorch.org/executorch)\n- [Helion](https://docs.pytorch.org/helion)\n- [torchao](https://docs.pytorch.org/ao)\n- [kineto](https://github.com/pytorch/kineto)\n- [torchtitan](https://github.com/pytorch/torchtitan)\n- [TorchRL](https://docs.pytorch.org/rl)\n- [torchvision](https://docs.pytorch.org/vision)\n- [torchaudio](https://docs.pytorch.org/audio)\n- [tensordict](https://docs.pytorch.org/tensordict)\n- [PyTorch on XLA Devices](https://docs.pytorch.org/xla)\n\n## Docs\n\nAccess comprehensive developer documentation for PyTorch\n\n[View Docs](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/index.html)\n\n## Tutorials\n\nGet in-depth tutorials for beginners and advanced developers\n\n[View Tutorials](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials)\n\n## Resources\n\nFind development resources and get your questions answered\n\n[View Resources](https://pytorch.org/resources)\n\nTo analyze traffic and optimize your experience, we serve cookies on this site. torch.nn.functional.scaled\\_dot\\_product\\_attention [\\#](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html\\#torch-nn-functional-scaled-dot-product-attention \"Link to this heading\")\n\ntorch.nn.functional.scaled\\_dot\\_product\\_attention() [\\[source\\]](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v2.14.0/torch/nn/functional.py#L6367) [#](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html#torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention \"Link to this definition\")scaled\\_dot\\_product\\_attention(query, key, value, attn\\_mask=None, dropout\\_p=0.0,\n\nis\\_causal=False, scale=None, enable\\_gqa=False) -> Tensor:\n\nComputes scaled dot product attention on query, key and value tensors, using an optional attention mask if passed,\nand applying dropout if a probability greater than 0.0 is specified. The optional scale argument can only be\nspecified as a keyword argument.\n\n```\n# Efficient implementation equivalent to the following:\ndef scaled_dot_product_attention(query, key, value, attn_mask=None, dropout_p=0.0,\n        is_causal=False, scale=None, enable_gqa=False) -> torch.Tensor:\n    L, S = query.size(-2), key.size(-2)\n    scale_factor = 1 / math.sqrt(query.size(-1)) if scale is None else scale\n    attn_bias = torch.zeros(L, S, dtype=query.dtype, device=query.device)\n    if is_causal:\n        assert attn_mask is None\n        temp_mask = torch.ones(L, S, dtype=torch.bool, device=query.device).tril(diagonal=0)\n        attn_bias.masked_fill_(temp_mask.logical_not(), float(\"-inf\"))\n\n    if attn_mask is not None:\n        if attn_mask.dtype == torch.bool:\n            attn_bias.masked_fill_(attn_mask.logical_not(), float(\"-inf\"))\n        else:\n            attn_bias = attn_mask + attn_bias\n\n    if enable_gqa:\n        key = key.repeat_interleave(query.size(-3)//key.size(-3), -3)\n        value = value.repeat_interleave(query.size(-3)//value.size(-3), -3)\n\n    attn_weight = query @ key.transpose(-2, -1) * scale_factor\n    attn_weight += attn_bias\n    attn_weight = torch.softmax(attn_weight, dim=-1)\n    attn_weight = torch.dropout(attn_weight, dropout_p, train=True)\n    return attn_weight @ value\n```\n\nCopy to clipboard\n\nWarning\n\nThis function is beta and subject to change.\n\nWarning\n\nThis function always applies dropout according to the specified `dropout_p` argument.\nTo disable dropout during evaluation, be sure to pass a value of `0.0` when the module\nthat makes the function call is not in training mode.\n\nFor example:\n\n```\nclass MyModel(nn.Module):\n    def __init__(self, p=0.5):\n        super().__init__()\n        self.p = p\n\n    def forward(self, ...):\n        return F.scaled_dot_product_attention(...,\n            dropout_p=(self.p if self.training else 0.0))\n```\n\nCopy to clipboard\n\nNote\n\nThe boolean mask semantics for `attn_mask` are the inverse of\n[`MultiheadAttention`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.MultiheadAttention.html#torch.nn.MultiheadAttention \"torch.nn.MultiheadAttention\")’s `key_padding_mask`.\n\nIn [`scaled_dot_product_attention()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html#torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention \"torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention\"), `True` indicates values\nto **participate** in attention.\n\nIn [`MultiheadAttention`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.MultiheadAttention.html#torch.nn.MultiheadAttention \"torch.nn.MultiheadAttention\"), `True` indicates values\nto be **masked out** (padding).\n\nIf migrating from MHA, ensure you invert your boolean mask (e.g.,\nusing `~mask` or `mask.logical_not()`).\n\nNote\n\nThere are currently three supported implementations of scaled dot product attention:\n\n> - [FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08691)\n>\n> - [Memory-Efficient Attention](https://github.com/facebookresearch/xformers)\n>\n> - A PyTorch implementation defined in C++ matching the above formulation\n\nThe function may call optimized kernels for improved performance when using the CUDA backend.\nFor all other backends, the PyTorch implementation will be used.\n\nAll implementations are enabled by default. Scaled dot product attention attempts to automatically select the\nmost optimal implementation based on the inputs. In order to provide more fine-grained control over what implementation\nis used, the following functions are provided for enabling and disabling implementations.\nThe context manager is the preferred mechanism:\n\n> - [`torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel.html#torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel \"torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel\"): A context manager used to enable or disable any of the implementations.\n>\n> - [`torch.backends.cuda.enable_flash_sdp()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/backends.html#torch.backends.cuda.enable_flash_sdp \"torch.backends.cuda.enable_flash_sdp\"): Globally enables or disables FlashAttention.\n>\n> - [`torch.backends.cuda.enable_mem_efficient_sdp()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/backends.html#torch.backends.cuda.enable_mem_efficient_sdp \"torch.backends.cuda.enable_mem_efficient_sdp\"): Globally enables or disables Memory-Efficient Attention.\n>\n> - [`torch.backends.cuda.enable_math_sdp()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/backends.html#torch.backends.cuda.enable_math_sdp \"torch.backends.cuda.enable_math_sdp\"): Globally enables or disables the PyTorch C++ implementation.\n\nEach of the fused kernels has specific input limitations. If the user requires the use of a specific fused implementation,\ndisable the PyTorch C++ implementation using [`torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel.html#torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel \"torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel\").\nIn the event that a fused implementation is not available, a warning will be raised with the\nreasons why the fused implementation cannot run.\n\nDue to the nature of fusing floating point operations, the output of this function may be different\ndepending on what backend kernel is chosen.\nThe c++ implementation supports torch.float64 and can be used when higher precision is required.\nFor math backend, all intermediates are kept in torch.float if inputs are in torch.half or torch.bfloat16.\n\nFor more information please see [Numerical accuracy](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/numerical_accuracy.html)\n\n> Grouped Query Attention (GQA) is an experimental feature. It works with FlashAttention,\n> cuDNN attention, and the math kernel on CUDA tensors. Memory-efficient attention also supports\n> GQA on NVIDIA CUDA. GQA does not support Nested tensors.\n> Constraints for GQA:\n>\n> > - number\\_of\\_heads\\_query % number\\_of\\_heads\\_key\\_value == 0 and,\n> >\n> > - number\\_of\\_heads\\_key == number\\_of\\_heads\\_value\n\nNote\n\nIn some circumstances when given tensors on a CUDA device and using CuDNN, this operator may select a nondeterministic algorithm to increase performance. If this is undesirable, you can try to make the operation deterministic (potentially at a performance cost) by setting `torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True`. See [Reproducibility](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/randomness.html) for more information.\n\nParameters:\n\n- **query** ( [_Tensor_](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/tensors.html#torch.Tensor \"torch.Tensor\")) – Query tensor; shape (N,...,Hq,L,E)(N, ..., Hq, L, E)(N,...,Hq,L,E).\n\n- **key** ( [_Tensor_](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/tensors.html#torch.Tensor \"torch.Tensor\")) – Key tensor; shape (N,...,H,S,E)(N, ..., H, S, E)(N,...,H,S,E).\n\n- **value** ( [_Tensor_](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/tensors.html#torch.Tensor \"torch.Tensor\")) – Value tensor; shape (N,...,H,S,Ev)(N, ..., H, S, Ev)(N,...,H,S,Ev).\n\n- **attn\\_mask** ( _optional Tensor_) – Attention mask; shape must be broadcastable to the shape of attention weights,\nwhich is (N,...,Hq,L,S)(N,..., Hq, L, S)(N,...,Hq,L,S). Two types of masks are supported.\nA boolean mask where a value of True indicates that the element _should_ take part in attention.\nA float mask of the same type as query, key, value that is added to the attention score.\n\n- **dropout\\_p** ( [_float_](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#float \"(in Python v3.14)\")) – Dropout probability; if greater than 0.0, dropout is applied\n\n- **is\\_causal** ( [_bool_](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#bool \"(in Python v3.14)\")) – If set to true, the attention masking is a lower triangular matrix when the mask is a\nsquare matrix. The attention masking has the form of the upper left causal bias due to the alignment\n(see [`torch.nn.attention.bias.CausalBias`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.attention.bias.CausalBias.html#torch.nn.attention.bias.CausalBias \"torch.nn.attention.bias.CausalBias\")) when the mask is a non-square matrix.\nAn error is thrown if both attn\\_mask and is\\_causal are set.\n\n- **scale** ( _optional python:float_ _,_ _keyword-only_) – Scaling factor applied prior to softmax. If None, the default value is set\nto 1E\\\\frac{1}{\\\\sqrt{E}}E​1​.\n\n- **enable\\_gqa** ( [_bool_](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#bool \"(in Python v3.14)\")) – If set to True, Grouped Query Attention (GQA) is enabled, by default it is set to False.\n\n\nReturns:\n\nAttention output; shape (N,...,Hq,L,Ev)(N, ..., Hq, L, Ev)(N,...,Hq,L,Ev).\n\nReturn type:\n\noutput ( [Tensor](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/tensors.html#torch.Tensor \"torch.Tensor\"))\n\nShape legend:\n\n- N:Batch size...:Any number of other batch dimensions (optional)N: \\\\text{Batch size} ... : \\\\text{Any number of other batch dimensions (optional)}N:Batch size...:Any number of other batch dimensions (optional)\n\n- S:Source sequence lengthS: \\\\text{Source sequence length}S:Source sequence length\n\n- L:Target sequence lengthL: \\\\text{Target sequence length}L:Target sequence length\n\n- E:Embedding dimension of the query and keyE: \\\\text{Embedding dimension of the query and key}E:Embedding dimension of the query and key\n\n- Ev:Embedding dimension of the valueEv: \\\\text{Embedding dimension of the value}Ev:Embedding dimension of the value\n\n- Hq:Number of heads of queryHq: \\\\text{Number of heads of query}Hq:Number of heads of query\n\n- H:Number of heads of key and valueH: \\\\text{Number of heads of key and value}H:Number of heads of key and value\n\n\nExamples\n\n```\n>>> # Optionally use the context manager to ensure one of the fused kernels is run\n>>> query = torch.rand(32, 8, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> key = torch.rand(32, 8, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> value = torch.rand(32, 8, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> with sdpa_kernel(backends=[SDPBackend.FLASH_ATTENTION]):\n>>>     F.scaled_dot_product_attention(query,key,value)\n```\n\nCopy to clipboard\n\n```\n>>> # Sample for GQA for llama3\n>>> query = torch.rand(32, 32, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> key = torch.rand(32, 8, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> value = torch.rand(32, 8, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> with sdpa_kernel(backends=[SDPBackend.MATH]):\n>>>     F.scaled_dot_product_attention(query,key,value,enable_gqa=True)\n```\n\nCopy to clipboard\n\nOn this page\n\n\n[Show Source](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/_sources/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.rst.txt)\n\nPyTorch Libraries\n\n- [ExecuTorch](https://docs.pytorch.org/executorch)\n- [Helion](https://docs.pytorch.org/helion)\n- [torchao](https://docs.pytorch.org/ao)\n- [kineto](https://github.com/pytorch/kineto)\n- [torchtitan](https://github.com/pytorch/torchtitan)\n- [TorchRL](https://docs.pytorch.org/rl)\n- [torchvision](https://docs.pytorch.org/vision)\n- [torchaudio](https://docs.pytorch.org/audio)\n- [tensordict](https://docs.pytorch.org/tensordict)\n- [PyTorch on XLA Devices](https://docs.pytorch.org/xla)\n\n## Docs\n\nAccess comprehensive developer documentation for PyTorch\n\n[View Docs](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/index.html)\n\n## Tutorials\n\nGet in-depth tutorials for beginners and advanced developers\n\n[View Tutorials](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials)\n\n## Resources\n\nFind development resources and get your questions answered\n\n[View Resources](https://pytorch.org/resources)\n\nTo analyze traffic and optimize your experience, we serve cookies on this site. torch.nn.functional.scaled\\_dot\\_product\\_attention [\\#](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html\\#torch-nn-functional-scaled-dot-product-attention \"Link to this heading\")\n\ntorch.nn.functional.scaled\\_dot\\_product\\_attention() [\\[source\\]](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v2.14.0/torch/nn/functional.py#L6367) [#](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html#torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention \"Link to this definition\")scaled\\_dot\\_product\\_attention(query, key, value, attn\\_mask=None, dropout\\_p=0.0,\n\nis\\_causal=False, scale=None, enable\\_gqa=False) -> Tensor:\n\nComputes scaled dot product attention on query, key and value tensors, using an optional attention mask if passed,\nand applying dropout if a probability greater than 0.0 is specified. The optional scale argument can only be\nspecified as a keyword argument.\n\n```\n# Efficient implementation equivalent to the following:\ndef scaled_dot_product_attention(query, key, value, attn_mask=None, dropout_p=0.0,\n        is_causal=False, scale=None, enable_gqa=False) -> torch.Tensor:\n    L, S = query.size(-2), key.size(-2)\n    scale_factor = 1 / math.sqrt(query.size(-1)) if scale is None else scale\n    attn_bias = torch.zeros(L, S, dtype=query.dtype, device=query.device)\n    if is_causal:\n        assert attn_mask is None\n        temp_mask = torch.ones(L, S, dtype=torch.bool, device=query.device).tril(diagonal=0)\n        attn_bias.masked_fill_(temp_mask.logical_not(), float(\"-inf\"))\n\n    if attn_mask is not None:\n        if attn_mask.dtype == torch.bool:\n            attn_bias.masked_fill_(attn_mask.logical_not(), float(\"-inf\"))\n        else:\n            attn_bias = attn_mask + attn_bias\n\n    if enable_gqa:\n        key = key.repeat_interleave(query.size(-3)//key.size(-3), -3)\n        value = value.repeat_interleave(query.size(-3)//value.size(-3), -3)\n\n    attn_weight = query @ key.transpose(-2, -1) * scale_factor\n    attn_weight += attn_bias\n    attn_weight = torch.softmax(attn_weight, dim=-1)\n    attn_weight = torch.dropout(attn_weight, dropout_p, train=True)\n    return attn_weight @ value\n```\n\nCopy to clipboard\n\nWarning\n\nThis function is beta and subject to change.\n\nWarning\n\nThis function always applies dropout according to the specified `dropout_p` argument.\nTo disable dropout during evaluation, be sure to pass a value of `0.0` when the module\nthat makes the function call is not in training mode.\n\nFor example:\n\n```\nclass MyModel(nn.Module):\n    def __init__(self, p=0.5):\n        super().__init__()\n        self.p = p\n\n    def forward(self, ...):\n        return F.scaled_dot_product_attention(...,\n            dropout_p=(self.p if self.training else 0.0))\n```\n\nCopy to clipboard\n\nNote\n\nThe boolean mask semantics for `attn_mask` are the inverse of\n[`MultiheadAttention`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.MultiheadAttention.html#torch.nn.MultiheadAttention \"torch.nn.MultiheadAttention\")’s `key_padding_mask`.\n\nIn [`scaled_dot_product_attention()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html#torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention \"torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention\"), `True` indicates values\nto **participate** in attention.\n\nIn [`MultiheadAttention`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.MultiheadAttention.html#torch.nn.MultiheadAttention \"torch.nn.MultiheadAttention\"), `True` indicates values\nto be **masked out** (padding).\n\nIf migrating from MHA, ensure you invert your boolean mask (e.g.,\nusing `~mask` or `mask.logical_not()`).\n\nNote\n\nThere are currently three supported implementations of scaled dot product attention:\n\n> - [FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08691)\n>\n> - [Memory-Efficient Attention](https://github.com/facebookresearch/xformers)\n>\n> - A PyTorch implementation defined in C++ matching the above formulation\n\nThe function may call optimized kernels for improved performance when using the CUDA backend.\nFor all other backends, the PyTorch implementation will be used.\n\nAll implementations are enabled by default. Scaled dot product attention attempts to automatically select the\nmost optimal implementation based on the inputs. In order to provide more fine-grained control over what implementation\nis used, the following functions are provided for enabling and disabling implementations.\nThe context manager is the preferred mechanism:\n\n> - [`torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel.html#torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel \"torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel\"): A context manager used to enable or disable any of the implementations.\n>\n> - [`torch.backends.cuda.enable_flash_sdp()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/backends.html#torch.backends.cuda.enable_flash_sdp \"torch.backends.cuda.enable_flash_sdp\"): Globally enables or disables FlashAttention.\n>\n> - [`torch.backends.cuda.enable_mem_efficient_sdp()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/backends.html#torch.backends.cuda.enable_mem_efficient_sdp \"torch.backends.cuda.enable_mem_efficient_sdp\"): Globally enables or disables Memory-Efficient Attention.\n>\n> - [`torch.backends.cuda.enable_math_sdp()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/backends.html#torch.backends.cuda.enable_math_sdp \"torch.backends.cuda.enable_math_sdp\"): Globally enables or disables the PyTorch C++ implementation.\n\nEach of the fused kernels has specific input limitations. If the user requires the use of a specific fused implementation,\ndisable the PyTorch C++ implementation using [`torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel.html#torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel \"torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel\").\nIn the event that a fused implementation is not available, a warning will be raised with the\nreasons why the fused implementation cannot run.\n\nDue to the nature of fusing floating point operations, the output of this function may be different\ndepending on what backend kernel is chosen.\nThe c++ implementation supports torch.float64 and can be used when higher precision is required.\nFor math backend, all intermediates are kept in torch.float if inputs are in torch.half or torch.bfloat16.\n\nFor more information please see [Numerical accuracy](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/numerical_accuracy.html)\n\n> Grouped Query Attention (GQA) is an experimental feature. It works with FlashAttention,\n> cuDNN attention, and the math kernel on CUDA tensors. Memory-efficient attention also supports\n> GQA on NVIDIA CUDA. GQA does not support Nested tensors.\n> Constraints for GQA:\n>\n> > - number\\_of\\_heads\\_query % number\\_of\\_heads\\_key\\_value == 0 and,\n> >\n> > - number\\_of\\_heads\\_key == number\\_of\\_heads\\_value\n\nNote\n\nIn some circumstances when given tensors on a CUDA device and using CuDNN, this operator may select a nondeterministic algorithm to increase performance. If this is undesirable, you can try to make the operation deterministic (potentially at a performance cost) by setting `torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True`. See [Reproducibility](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/randomness.html) for more information.\n\nParameters:\n\n- **query** ( [_Tensor_](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/tensors.html#torch.Tensor \"torch.Tensor\")) – Query tensor; shape (N,...,Hq,L,E)(N, ..., Hq, L, E)(N,...,Hq,L,E).\n\n- **key** ( [_Tensor_](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/tensors.html#torch.Tensor \"torch.Tensor\")) – Key tensor; shape (N,...,H,S,E)(N, ..., H, S, E)(N,...,H,S,E).\n\n- **value** ( [_Tensor_](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/tensors.html#torch.Tensor \"torch.Tensor\")) – Value tensor; shape (N,...,H,S,Ev)(N, ..., H, S, Ev)(N,...,H,S,Ev).\n\n- **attn\\_mask** ( _optional Tensor_) – Attention mask; shape must be broadcastable to the shape of attention weights,\nwhich is (N,...,Hq,L,S)(N,..., Hq, L, S)(N,...,Hq,L,S). Two types of masks are supported.\nA boolean mask where a value of True indicates that the element _should_ take part in attention.\nA float mask of the same type as query, key, value that is added to the attention score.\n\n- **dropout\\_p** ( [_float_](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#float \"(in Python v3.14)\")) – Dropout probability; if greater than 0.0, dropout is applied\n\n- **is\\_causal** ( [_bool_](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#bool \"(in Python v3.14)\")) – If set to true, the attention masking is a lower triangular matrix when the mask is a\nsquare matrix. The attention masking has the form of the upper left causal bias due to the alignment\n(see [`torch.nn.attention.bias.CausalBias`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.attention.bias.CausalBias.html#torch.nn.attention.bias.CausalBias \"torch.nn.attention.bias.CausalBias\")) when the mask is a non-square matrix.\nAn error is thrown if both attn\\_mask and is\\_causal are set.\n\n- **scale** ( _optional python:float_ _,_ _keyword-only_) – Scaling factor applied prior to softmax. If None, the default value is set\nto 1E\\\\frac{1}{\\\\sqrt{E}}E​1​.\n\n- **enable\\_gqa** ( [_bool_](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#bool \"(in Python v3.14)\")) – If set to True, Grouped Query Attention (GQA) is enabled, by default it is set to False.\n\n\nReturns:\n\nAttention output; shape (N,...,Hq,L,Ev)(N, ..., Hq, L, Ev)(N,...,Hq,L,Ev).\n\nReturn type:\n\noutput ( [Tensor](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/tensors.html#torch.Tensor \"torch.Tensor\"))\n\nShape legend:\n\n- N:Batch size...:Any number of other batch dimensions (optional)N: \\\\text{Batch size} ... : \\\\text{Any number of other batch dimensions (optional)}N:Batch size...:Any number of other batch dimensions (optional)\n\n- S:Source sequence lengthS: \\\\text{Source sequence length}S:Source sequence length\n\n- L:Target sequence lengthL: \\\\text{Target sequence length}L:Target sequence length\n\n- E:Embedding dimension of the query and keyE: \\\\text{Embedding dimension of the query and key}E:Embedding dimension of the query and key\n\n- Ev:Embedding dimension of the valueEv: \\\\text{Embedding dimension of the value}Ev:Embedding dimension of the value\n\n- Hq:Number of heads of queryHq: \\\\text{Number of heads of query}Hq:Number of heads of query\n\n- H:Number of heads of key and valueH: \\\\text{Number of heads of key and value}H:Number of heads of key and value\n\n\nExamples\n\n```\n>>> # Optionally use the context manager to ensure one of the fused kernels is run\n>>> query = torch.rand(32, 8, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> key = torch.rand(32, 8, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> value = torch.rand(32, 8, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> with sdpa_kernel(backends=[SDPBackend.FLASH_ATTENTION]):\n>>>     F.scaled_dot_product_attention(query,key,value)\n```\n\nCopy to clipboard\n\n```\n>>> # Sample for GQA for llama3\n>>> query = torch.rand(32, 32, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> key = torch.rand(32, 8, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> value = torch.rand(32, 8, 128, 64, dtype=torch.float16, device=\"cuda\")\n>>> with sdpa_kernel(backends=[SDPBackend.MATH]):\n>>>     F.scaled_dot_product_attention(query,key,value,enable_gqa=True)\n```\n\nCopy to clipboard\n\nOn this page\n\n\n[Show Source](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/_sources/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.rst.txt)\n\nPyTorch Libraries\n\n- [ExecuTorch](https://docs.pytorch.org/executorch)\n- [Helion](https://docs.pytorch.org/helion)\n- [torchao](https://docs.pytorch.org/ao)\n- [kineto](https://github.com/pytorch/kineto)\n- [torchtitan](https://github.com/pytorch/torchtitan)\n- [TorchRL](https://docs.pytorch.org/rl)\n- [torchvision](https://docs.pytorch.org/vision)\n- [torchaudio](https://docs.pytorch.org/audio)\n- [tensordict](https://docs.pytorch.org/tensordict)\n- [PyTorch on XLA Devices](https://docs.pytorch.org/xla)\n\n## Docs\n\nAccess comprehensive developer documentation for PyTorch\n\n[View Docs](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/index.html)\n\n## Tutorials\n\nGet in-depth tutorials for beginners and advanced developers\n\n[View Tutorials](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials)\n\n## Resources\n\nFind development resources and get your questions answered\n\n[View Resources](https://pytorch.org/resources)\n\nTo analyze traffic and optimize your experience, we serve cookies on this site. attention on query, key and value tensors, using an optional attention mask if passed,\nand applying dropout if a probability greater than 0.0 is specified. The optional scale argument can only be\nspecified as a keyword argument.\n\n```\n# Efficient implementation equivalent to the following:\ndef scaled_dot_product_attention(query, key, value, attn_mask=None, dropout_p=0.0,\n        is_causal=False, scale=None, enable_gqa=False) -> torch.Tensor:\n    L, S = query.size(-2), key.size(-2)\n    scale_factor = 1 / math.sqrt(query.size(-1)) if scale is None else scale\n    attn_bias = torch.zeros(L, S, dtype=query.dtype, device=query.device)\n    if is_causal:\n        assert attn_mask is None\n        temp_mask = torch.ones(L, S, dtype=torch.bool, device=query.device).tril(diagonal=0)\n        attn_bias.masked_fill_(temp_mask.logical_not(), float(\"-inf\"))\n\n    if attn_mask is not None:\n        if attn_mask.dtype == torch.bool:\n            attn_bias.masked_fill_(attn_mask.logical_not(), float(\"-inf\"))\n        else:\n            attn_bias = attn_mask + attn_bias\n\n    if enable_gqa:\n        key = key.repeat_interleave(query.size(-3)//key.size(-3), -3)\n        value = value.repeat_interleave(query.size(-3)//value.size(-3), -3)\n\n    attn_weight = query @ key.transpose(-2, -1) * scale_factor\n    attn_weight += attn_bias\n    attn_weight = torch.softmax(attn_weight, dim=-1)\n    attn_weight = torch.dropout(attn_weight, dropout_p, train=True)\n    return attn_weight @ value\n```\n\nCopy to evaluation, be sure to pass a value of `0.0` when the module\nthat makes the function call is not in training mode.\n\nFor example:\n\n```\nclass MyModel(nn.Module):\n    def __init__(self, p=0.5):\n        super().__init__()\n        self.p = p\n\n    def forward(self, ...):\n        return F.scaled_dot_product_attention(...,\n            dropout_p=(self.p if self.training else 0.0))\n```\n\nCopy Yes. You’re close enough to Hugging Face’s speed on your Mac that I’d stop guessing which operation is slow and work through a few measured changes.

1. **Make the benchmark more revealing.** Your current benchmark uses one short prompt, one request, and a 16-token cache block. Test short and long prompts, 32–256 generated tokens, and 1–4 concurrent requests. Track time to first token, decode tokens/second, and memory separately. Also, the custom-model benchmark synchronizes MPS after *every* `Engine.step()`, while the Hugging Face path does not; I’d measure an end-to-end run with synchronization only at the timing boundaries as well as the current per-step run. [PyTorch notes that forcing MPS operations to complete individually can hurt performance.](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.mps.profiler.profile.html)

2. **Reduce KV-cache work during prefill.** [`PagedKVCache.append()`](./utils/kv_cache.py:209) writes one token at a time. For a prefill chunk, group consecutive tokens destined for the same physical block and write each slice together. Decode still writes just one token, so this primarily targets prompt processing. Test writes that cross block boundaries and touch shared prefix blocks.

3. **Measure the small operations repeated in every layer.** [`RMSNorm`](./utils/layers.py:4) performs several separate tensor operations, and [`RotaryEmbedding`](./utils/layers.py:18) recomputes inverse frequencies each forward pass. A low-risk experiment is to cache the inverse frequencies; a separate experiment is to compare your RMSNorm with [PyTorch’s `rms_norm`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.functional.rms_norm.html). Keep either change only if it preserves output accuracy *and* improves measured speed.

4. **Improve cached attention for multiple requests and long contexts.** Your current path gathers blocks, concatenates K/V, and repeats KV heads before attention. That was a good speed win for the short-prompt case, but those copies may grow with context length. Benchmark where it stops winning. A later, harder project would be a Metal kernel that reads the block table directly, avoiding the gather. [PyTorch provides a way to invoke custom Metal shaders](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.mps.compile_shader.html), but I would only build one after a longer-context benchmark identifies attention as the bottleneck. I would **not** assume `enable_gqa=True` solves the head repetition on MPS; [the PyTorch 2.14 documentation describes GQA support for CUDA backends](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html).

5. **Separate model speed from streaming overhead.** [`stream_output()`](./utils/engine.py:184) decodes the *entire* generated sequence after every token. That can become increasingly costly for long outputs. Benchmark with and without text streaming, then consider incremental decoding if it matters.

My recommended next move is **a benchmark matrix first, then block-wise KV writes**. It gives you evidence about where to spend effort, followed by a concrete optimization that fits the engine you’ve already built. I wouldn’t change the 500×500 default cache configuration or jump to quantization yet.

Your engine is **roughly at Hugging Face parity for decode**, not consistently faster yet. It wins 7 of 8 decode rows, but the median advantage is only about 2–3%; the 22-token, 64-output, batch-1 case is 12% slower. I wouldn’t call that a reliable speedup from this run alone.

The clearer pattern is time to first token: your engine is slower in most rows, particularly with the 132-token prompt. That points toward prefill as the next performance area to measure. Batch size 2 improves *total* throughput for both implementations, so batching is paying off.

I’d investigate the two `token match: False` rows **before optimizing further**. Both occur at prompt length 132 and batch size 2. The [benchmark comparison](./benchmark.py:164) marks the whole row false if *any repeat* differs—even if two Hugging Face repeats differ from each other. It also compares Hugging Face’s full returned token rows with your requests’ stopped token lists; padding after EOS could produce a false mismatch. The table alone cannot distinguish those cases from a real model divergence.

Next, print the generated-token count and first differing token position for each request and repeat. If the difference is only after EOS, fix the comparison. If it occurs before EOS, compare first-token logits for the 132-token batch of two, then inspect the batched prefill and cached-attention paths. For speed, rerun with `--repeats 3` or more; the current small advantages are within a range where run-to-run variation matters.

The best next target is **prefill**, because your longer prompts consistently have higher time to first token than Hugging Face.

1. **Avoid computing vocabulary logits for every prompt position.** [Model.forward](./utils/model.py:46) applies `lm_head` to the whole sequence, but [Engine.process_prefill_batch](./utils/engine.py:208) only samples from each request’s final prompt position. Project just those final hidden states when a request finishes prefill; intermediate chunks need no logits. I’d try this first.

2. **Benchmark the existing prefill SDPA switch.** Run the same matrix with `--sdpa` and without it. Your cached prefill currently uses the manual attention path by default, so this is a small experiment before rewriting attention.

3. **Batch cached attention across requests.** [SelfAttention.forward](./utils/attention.py:84) loops over requests inside every layer, gathering and attending separately. A same-length decode fast path could process several requests together. This targets multi-request throughput, but is a more involved change.

4. **Measure real prefix-cache reuse.** The matrix adds identical requests simultaneously, before either has populated the cache. Add a separate warm-prefix case where one request finishes prefill before the next arrives. That will show whether caching actually improves TTFT.

I’d do **#1, then measure #2**. I’d hold off on custom Metal kernels or quantization until the benchmark identifies a larger, repeatable bottleneck; the recent decode differences have been too variable to justify either yet.

I reviewed the inference path and ran the repository’s MPS profiler. The main gap to vLLM/Ollama-class performance is now the compute backend, not the scheduler. Your engine is close to Hugging Face’s eager path in some batch-2 cases, but it still moves full-precision weights and reconstructs cached attention data on every token.

I’d tackle the next work in this order:

1. **Remove wasted decode work.** [DecodeBatch](./utils/batch.py:39) builds a padding mask and a context-length attention mask every token. Neither is read by the cached single-token attention paths. Skip their construction, and make [Model.forward](./utils/model.py:48) avoid creating a replacement mask for cached decode. This is a small, testable change.

2. **Measure lower-precision weights.** [model_loader()](./utils/model_loader.py:13) inherits the reference weights’ dtype; the profiled run occupied about **6.6 GiB on MPS**. Benchmark FP16 against the current model for memory, TTFT, and decode speed, while checking output quality. Don’t assume exact token-for-token parity after changing precision.

3. **Stop gathering the entire KV history for decode.** [get_batch()](./utils/kv_cache.py:263) copies blocks into contiguous tensors every layer and token. The fast path in [SelfAttention](./utils/attention.py:91) also requires equal request positions; mixed-length requests fall back to individual reads. A Metal paged-attention kernel that reads block tables directly is the substantial next attention project.

4. **Move toward quantized, fused matrix operations.** Q/K/V and gate/up are separate projections in [attention.py](./utils/attention.py:11) and [layers.py](./utils/layers.py:52). Fusing projections can cut launches; *fused quantized* matrix operations can also cut weight traffic. Merely storing 4-bit weights and expanding them to FP32 each token would miss much of the benefit. Current Apple-Silicon-oriented backends provide useful reference designs: [MLX quantized layers](https://ml-explore.github.io/mlx/build/html/python/_autosummary/mlx.nn.quantize.html) and [llama.cpp’s Metal/quantization support](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/wiki/Feature-matrix). vLLM’s Apple GPU route likewise uses an [MLX-based Metal plugin](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/getting_started/installation/cpu/index.html?device=apple).

5. **Fix long, mixed-length prefill.** [PrefillBatch](./utils/batch.py:5) pads every request to the longest chunk and materializes a dense attention mask. Packed/variable-length prefill would avoid computing padded tokens and should matter much more for realistic traffic than the current identical-prompt matrix suggests.

Before claiming parity with Ollama, extend [benchmark.py](./benchmark.py:178) to use mixed prompts and arrival times, and compare the same model, precision, context, and batch size. Its current identical-prompt cases favor your equal-length fast path. Also, the default `500 × 500` KV-cache allocation in [Engine](./utils/engine.py:19) works out to about **53.4 GiB** for Qwen3-1.7B at FP32; the benchmark overrides it, so its results do not expose that default.

The profiler recorded 9,358 `copy_` calls, but it collected CPU activity—not MPS kernel duration—so I would use [MPS signposts](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.15/generated/torch.mps.profiler.profile.html) before choosing a kernel to rewrite. **My recommended next implementation is item 1, followed by a controlled FP16 benchmark.** No files were changed in this review.

I removed the unused cached-decode masks and added an opt-in FP16 benchmark mode. FP16 stays opt-in because lower precision can change outputs.

On your Mac MPS, the loaded custom model used **3.22 GiB in FP16 vs 6.44 GiB in FP32**. Across the four 32-token matrix cases, FP16 decode was about **1.7–1.8× faster** than the FP32 custom model; all generated tokens matched the FP32 Hugging Face reference. The 132-token prompt, batch-2, 64-output case also matched across three repeats and reached **39.64 decode tokens/s** in FP16 versus **22.76** for Hugging Face FP32. These are measurements for this workload, not a guarantee for other prompts.

The affected tests passed (**79/79**), and `git diff --check` is clean. The usage is in [README.md](./README.md). I left the larger paged-attention kernel and quantized-backend work untouched; those need their own implementation and validation.

> Any further improvements you can see can be made?

Yes. After the FP16 gain, I’d prioritize these:

1. **Fix text streaming overhead.** [Engine.stream_output](./utils/engine.py:186) decodes *all* generated tokens after every new token. That grows quadratically with output length. The matrix benchmark has streaming off, so it hides this cost. Use a tokenizer-safe incremental buffer; decoding each token independently can break spaces or Unicode.

2. **Improve mixed-length batches.** The fast [batched attention path](./utils/attention.py:91) only runs when requests have the same position. Real requests usually differ. Supporting variable-length batched decode—and eventually reading block tables directly in a Metal kernel—is likely the largest remaining attention gain.

3. **Reduce model kernel launches.** Fuse Q/K/V projections and gate/up projections, then investigate fused RMSNorm and residual operations. The profile counted 3,616 RMSNorm calls in one 32-step batch-2 run. Benchmark each fusion independently; fewer operations do not always mean faster MPS execution.

4. **Pack prefill instead of padding.** [PrefillBatch](./utils/batch.py:5) computes up to the longest request in a batch. Mixed short and long prompts can waste substantial work. This matters more for TTFT and throughput under realistic traffic than for the identical-prompt benchmark.

I’d implement **streaming first for real serving performance**, then build a mixed-prompt benchmark before tackling variable-length attention. For a large jump toward Ollama-like single-request speed, fused quantized Metal/MLX compute remains the bigger project.

Implemented the four optimizations. Streaming now decodes new tokens incrementally; cached decode can batch requests at different positions; QKV and MLP projections can be fused with `--fuse-projections`; and prefill can use optional length bucketing to reduce padding. The main changes are in [engine.py](./utils/engine.py), [attention.py](./utils/attention.py), and [benchmark.py](./benchmark.py).

On the mixed-length MPS benchmark, bucketing reduced time to first token from about 0.345s to 0.271s, while mixed-length batched decode improved decode throughput from 37.55 to 38.95 tokens/s. Token outputs matched. Fusion showed a smaller ~2% gain in one run, so I’d treat that as provisional.

The affected engine, cache, and model tests pass (188 tests), and `git diff --check` is clean. This uses length bucketing—not fully packed prefill—and does not yet include a custom Metal paged-attention kernel.

> # `x-gpt2-tokenizer`
> Loading a real GPT-2 tokenizer from HuggingFace model files. This example downloads GPT-2's vocabulary and merges, builds the full byte-level BPE pipeline, and demonstrates encoding, decoding, and subword inspection.
>
> ## What You'll Learn
> - Decoding token IDs back to text
>
> ## Key Functions
> | Function | Purpose |
> |-|-|
> | `Pre_tokenizer.byte_level` | GPT-2 style byte-level pre-tokenizer |
> | `Decoder.byte_level` | Corresponding byte-level decoder |
> | `Brot.decode` | Decode token IDs back to text |
> | `Encoding.tokens` | Token strings from an encoding |
> | `Encoding.ids` | Token IDs from an encoding |
>
> ## Prerequisites
> This example downloads GPT-2 model files from HuggingFace on first run (~1 MB total). Files are cached in `/tmp/brot_gpt2/`.
