The benchmark runs end to end on your Mac’s MPS device, and every measured case matched Hugging Face’s generated token IDs. I made no code changes during this verification.

The key finding is about dtype. The benchmark’s default reference load produced **FP32** weights. With the custom model also using that source dtype, the 132-token prompt, batch-two case was effectively tied: **22.11 HF vs 21.75 custom decode tokens/s**. The earlier ~1.8× custom speedup used FP16 custom weights against FP32 HF weights, so it is not a fair engine-to-engine comparison.

I’d prioritize the next work this way:

1. **Fix the benchmark comparison first:** load both models at the same explicit dtype and print their actual weight dtypes. Otherwise optimizations are hard to evaluate.
2. **Target cached decode:** batched `gather_sdpa` reached ~40–41 tokens/s in the FP16 batch-two test, versus ~15–16 for the Python direct-paged path. Keep `gather_sdpa` as the MPS default. The larger opportunity is a kernel that reads [KV blocks](./utils/kv_cache.py:267) directly without gathering the full prefix into new tensors each token.
3. **Measure mixed-length prefill:** [PrefillBatch](./utils/batch.py:4) still pads to the longest request and builds a dense mask. Add mixed-length cases and the existing bucketing option to the benchmark before attempting packed prefill.
4. **Profile per-token overhead:** [Engine sampling](./utils/engine.py:198) brings token IDs back to Python each step, while cache appends and scheduling also run per token. A profiler will show which of these is worth reducing.

One environment note: the Conda benchmark ran on CPU because MPS was unavailable there; I used the Python 3.12 environment with MPS access for the results above.

The measured improvement is now on by default: [Engine](./utils/engine.py) buckets mixed-length prefill requests when padding would be substantial. On MPS, simultaneous 22- and 132-token prompts improved from **0.410s to 0.344s time to first token** (~16%), with matching output tokens.

I also updated [benchmark.py](./benchmark.py) to match and print both models’ weight dtypes, and added a mixed-length comparison mode. With both models at FP32, the 132-token, batch-two decode result was effectively tied: **24.10 HF vs 23.82 custom tokens/s**. A short matched-FP16 run also matched tokens.

I tested a batched KV-write change, but alternating MPS runs showed no reliable gain, so I reverted it. The next substantial decode improvement would need a direct paged-attention kernel; the Python direct path is slower than the current gather/SDPA path on MPS.

Verification: **246 tests passed, 1 skipped**; the final targeted tests also passed.

> Based on the results, and goign through the code, what other improvements can be made

<details><summary>2 previous messages</summary>

> I’ll review the current hot paths against the benchmark results, then rank improvements by likely payoff and implementation risk. I’ll distinguish changes supported by these measurements from ideas that still need profiling.
>
> <details><summary>Explored 5 files, 2 searches</summary>

> - Read `./profile_engine.py`

> - Searched for `hidden_size|vocab_size|intermediate_size|tie_word_embeddings` in `config.json`
>
> </details>
</details>

The next gains are likely in GPU memory movement and kernel launches, not the scheduler. The fair FP32 benchmark was effectively tied with Hugging Face, while mixed-length bucketing improved first-token time by about 16%.

I’d pursue these in order:

1. **Avoid copying the KV history on every decode token.** [get_batch()](./utils/kv_cache.py:267) gathers and makes K/V contiguous for every layer and token. At the measured 132-token, batch-two FP32 size, that is roughly 60 MB of K/V data per decode step before additional copies. A Metal attention kernel that reads block-table entries directly is the largest architectural opportunity. The existing Python direct-paged path is slower, so switching to it is not the fix.

2. **Profile weight reads and test weight-only quantization.** This model’s tied embedding/output matrix alone has about 311 million weights. FP16 halved loaded model memory from 6.44 to 3.22 GiB in our runs. Quantization could help further, but only if dequantization is fused into the matrix multiplication; converting entire weights each token would defeat the purpose.

3. **Move from bucketing to genuinely packed prefill.** [PrefillBatch](./utils/batch.py:4) still computes padded positions and a dense mask within each bucket. The measured bucketing gain shows this is worth exploring for mixed prompt lengths.

4. **Reduce small-kernel launches.** [RMSNorm and RoPE](./utils/layers.py:4) each use several tensor operations, repeated through 28 layers. Fused kernels may matter most for short prompts and small batches, but this needs MPS profiling before implementation.

I would **not** prioritize batched KV writes: the A/B test showed no reliable gain, so I reverted that change. The best next experiment is to profile short and long decode separately, then tackle direct block-table attention or fused weight operations based on where MPS actually spends its time.

> ## [issue:bitsandbytes-foundation/bitsandbytes#2011] (issue) Offer to help improve the MPS backend fallbacks#2011
> https://github.com/bitsandbytes-foundation/bitsandbytes/issues/2011
> # Offer to help improve the MPS backend fallbacks#2011
> ## Description
> Thanks for asking!
>
> The README's 🐢 is a little out of date. With the newer Hub kernels the 4bit quantize/dequantize/gemv ops are in a much better place.
>
> I'll be implementing it similar to the CPU backend, which will rely on the separate `quantize_blockwise`, `dequantize_blockwise` ops, and do the rest in PyTorch. I think this will be good enough to start before jumping further to e.g. a fully fused kernel like we have on the CUDA side.
>
> Another op that I know has room for improvement is `quantize_blockwise`.
>
> I have not quite figured out exactly how I want to bring additional Metal kernels to the project in the future. I'm leaning on using `torch.mps.compile_shader` for this and doing JIT. The `compile_shader` approach avoids all of that.
>
> I took your `compile_shader` lean and the `quantize_blockwise` note as the starting point and have some numbers from an M5 (10-core GPU, macOS 26, torch 2.12.1, no `kernels` package installed so this is purely the fallback path). Input is a 4096x4096 fp32 tensor, blocksize 256, dynamic map, 20 timed iterations after warmup with `torch.mps.synchronize()`.
>
> | `quantize_blockwise` variant | time |
> |-|-|
> | current MPS fallback (binary search over bounds) | 6.9 ms |
> | same, with `torch.compile` | 6.9 ms |
> | `torch.bucketize` (default backend path) | 2488 ms |
> | `torch.searchsorted` | 2283 ms |
> | fused Metal kernel via `torch.mps.compile_shader` | 1.6 ms |
>
> 2. The Metal kernel is a single `compile_shader` source, no libtorch linkage, no build changes. One threadgroup of 256 threads per block: `simd_max` reduction for the block absmax, then each thread scales its elements and does the same binary search over `(code[i] + code[i+1]) / 2` bounds that the fallback does, so it reproduces `bucketize` semantics exactly. On the 4096x4096 input the output bytes and absmax match the current fallback bit for bit. The shader is compiled once and cached at module level, so the JIT cost is paid on first call only. I've only run it at blocksize 256 so far; other blocksizes need a small loop change and I would guard the whole thing on `hasattr(torch.mps, "compile_shader")` so torch 2.4 through 2.6 keep the current fallback.
>
> I had timed the absmax reduction in eager mode, but `_quantize_blockwise_compute` is already wrapped in `_try_torch_compile`, and on this setup the compile succeeds and inductor fuses the abs and the max. For reference, the eager path is ~80 ms on the same input (the binary search dominates), so the existing compile wrapper is doing most of the work.
>
> The rest of the table stands: the Metal `compile_shader` kernel at 1.6 ms was compared against the compiled fallback, and `bucketize` is 2.3 s eager or compiled.
>
> I went ahead and built the `compile_shader` kernel for `quantize_blockwise` as a prototype so the discussion has something concrete behind it. It's on a branch, not a PR, since you said you hadn't settled how you want Metal kernels brought in: egeozkoc/bitsandbytes@feature/mps-metal-quantize-blockwise.
>
> The open question is still how you want this structured: I put the shader source in a separate `backends/mps/shaders.py` with a lazily compiled, process-cached library, but if you'd rather have the source inline in `ops.py`, or a different caching or fallback policy, or want it to cover `quantize_4bit` and `dequantize_blockwise` in the same pass, say which and I'll reshape it.
>
> ## [doc:https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/0f53828e83f2212060233d2ea552cc76617b8712/docs/source/en/apple_silicon.md] (doc) Apple Silicon
> # Apple Silicon
> Apple Silicon (M-series) chips run PyTorch through the Metal Performance Shaders (MPS) backend, with the device string `mps`.
>
> MPS works with the standard `torch` install. Check that PyTorch was built with MPS and can see the GPU.
>
> ## Quantize models
> Metal quantizes a model when you load it, while GGUF runs checkpoints that are already quantized.
>
> - Metal quantizes to 2, 4, or 8 bits with Metal kernels from the Hub.
> - GGUF keeps weights packed on MPS when the `ggml-org/ggml-quantization` kernel is available.
> - bitsandbytes quantizes to 4 bits with native MPS kernels.
>
> ## Train with Trainer
> [`TrainingArguments`] detects MPS and sets the device to `mps`, so [`Trainer`] trains on it without any device settings.
>
> It prints `mps` when `Trainer` will train on the GPU.
>
> ### Limit graph cache growth
> MPS compiles a Metal kernel for each tensor shape it sees and keeps them in a graph cache that is never evicted.
>
> ## Next steps
> - Read the PyTorch MPS backend notes for supported operations and known issues.
> - Check the Metal column in the quantization overview to find every quantization method that runs on MPS.
>
> ## [readme:tashiscool/fp8-mps-metal] (readme) tashiscool/fp8-mps-metal
> https://github.com/tashiscool/fp8-mps-metal
> # fp8-mps-metal
> **Custom FP8 compute kernels for Apple Silicon (MPS) — fixing what PyTorch doesn't support yet.**
>
> This repo contains a Metal compute shader that performs FP8 (e4m3fn) dequantization and matrix multiplication directly on the GPU, exposed to PyTorch as a drop-in monkey-patch.
>
> **Tested on:** M4 Pro (48GB), macOS 26.2, PyTorch 2.10.0, Python 3.12
>
> ## Quick Start
> The Metal shader compiles at runtime via `torch.mps.compile_shader()`.
>
> ## What This Solves
> | What works | What doesn't | Impact |
> |-|-|-|
> | Create FP8 tensors | Cast float32 → FP8 on MPS | Can't quantize on-device |
> | Transfer FP8 CPU → MPS | `torch._scaled_mm` on MPS | **FLUX/SD3.5 won't run** |
>
> This repo provides 4 Metal GPU kernels:
>
> 3. **`fp8_to_half_kernel`** — FP8 → FP16 dequantization
>
> # Why Things Don't Work on Mac (NVIDIA → Apple Silicon Guide)
> ## What Fails (and Why)
> ### 1. FP8 (float8_e4m3fn / float8_e5m2) — SOLVED BY THIS REPO
> PyTorch's MPS backend never implemented the cast or compute kernels for FP8.
>
> ## [doc:https://pytorch.org/blog/pytorch-2-14-release-blog/] (doc) PyTorch 2.14 Release Blog
> # PyTorch 2.14 Release Blog
> PyTorch 2.14 builds directly on those threads.
>
> Apple Silicon users benefit from native linear-algebra routines (SVD, QR, Cholesky, and more) and a broad migration to hand-tuned Metal kernels that cut overhead on Mac GPUs.
>
> ## Performance Improvements
> ### Large MPS Op Migration to Native Metal
> Continuing the migration begun in 2.13, a further set of MPS operators moved off Apple’s MPSGraph framework onto hand-written Metal compute kernels, including `index_add`, `index_select`, `argmin`, `argmax`, `conv3d`, `median`, `nanmedian`, `linspace`, `arange`, `nan_to_num`, `log_sigmoid`, `sigmoid_backward`, `mish` and GLU.
>
> Reductions received a dedicated five-part rewrite covering full reductions, inner-dimension reductions, strided and batched outer reductions, small-dimension and narrow kernels, and the `argmax` and `argmin` split-K paths.
>
> The native Metal path eliminates MPSGraph’s per-op compilation cost and gives PyTorch direct control over thread dispatch and memory access patterns, reducing kernel launch latency across common training and inference workloads on Apple Silicon.
>
> API Unstable
>
> ### MPS Memory and Copy Paths

>
> ### F.linear Decode Path on MPS

> # [Discussion] How to add MPS extension with custom kernel?#81103
> ## Description
> ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
> Hi,
>
> I am working on adding MPS op for MPS backend with a custom kernel.
>
> Here is an example:
>
> [https://github.com/grimoire/TorchMPSCustomOpsDemo](https://github.com/grimoire/TorchMPSCustomOpsDemo)
>
> I am new to Metal. I am not sure if it is a good way (or the right way) to add such op. There are something I want to discuss:
>
> ## Device and CommandQueue
> Since PyTorch has not exposed the MPS-related API, I have to copy some head from torch csrc. The library is build with `MPSDevice::getInstance()->device()` and the command is commit to `getCurrentMPSStream()`. I am not sure if I should flush on commit or not.
>
> ## LibraryFromUrl vs LibraryFromSource
> So I have to:
>
> Either load it at runtime, which leads to the problem of how to find the relative location of the `.metallib`.
>
> ## BuildExtension
> If we does not build metal kernel at runtime, we need to setup the compiler for metal kernel in the `setup.py`.
>
> Since the `build_ext` provided by Python and PyTorch does not support build Metal, I patched the `UnixCCompiler` in `BuildExtension` to add the support. Both `compile` and `link` need to be updated:
>

> # [MPS] compile_shader cannot resolve c10/metal headers with a scikit-build-core editable install#195293
> ## Description
> ### 🐛 Describe the bug
> With a scikit-build-core editable install (`pip install -e . --no-build-isolation`), `torch.mps.compile_shader` cannot resolve any `c10/metal` header, so every shader that includes one fails to compile.
>
> The headers are installed, but not where `compile_shader` looks: they land in `site-packages/torch/include/c10/metal/`, while `import torch` resolves to the source checkout, and the include directory is computed relative to `torch.__file__`.
>
> ### Versions
> macOS 15 on Apple silicon, `main` at `1d18a51`, built with `pip install -e . --no-build-isolation`, Python 3.12.

> # fp8-mps-metal
> **Custom FP8 compute kernels for Apple Silicon (MPS) — fixing what PyTorch doesn't support yet.**
>
> This repo contains a Metal compute shader that performs FP8 (e4m3fn) dequantization and matrix multiplication directly on the GPU, exposed to PyTorch as a drop-in monkey-patch.
>
> **Tested on:** M4 Pro (48GB), macOS 26.2, PyTorch 2.10.0, Python 3.12
>
> ## Quick Start
>
> The Metal shader compiles at runtime via `torch.mps.compile_shader()`.
>
> ## What This Solves
> | What works | What doesn't | Impact |
> |-|-|-|
> | Transfer FP8 CPU → MPS | `torch._scaled_mm` on MPS | **FLUX/SD3.5 won't run** |
>
> # Why Things Don't Work on Mac (NVIDIA → Apple Silicon Guide)
> ## Architecture
>
> ## System Requirements
> - PyTorch 2.4+ (for `torch._scaled_mm`), 2.10+ recommended (for `torch.mps.compile_shader`)

> ## [issue:pytorch/pytorch#152155] (issue) torch.compile on MPS fails: generated Metal kernel uses loop-local variable out of scope#152155
> https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/152155
> # torch.compile on MPS fails: generated Metal kernel uses loop-local variable out of scope#152155
>
> ## Description
>
> ### 🐛 Describe the bug
>
> I'm a total newcomer to PyTorch programming. I encountered this bug while trying to run the example code for nari-labs/dia on my M2 Mac.
>
> When I ran the example using torch.compile(...), I hit a compile-time error from TorchInductor's Metal backend. Since I wasn't sure how to interpret the error, I asked ChatGPT (GPT-4o) for help. I shared the full error message and even pasted the contents of torch/\_inductor/codegen/mps.py, and we discussed where the bug might be coming from.
>
> Sorry in advance if this is a duplicate.
>
> I just hope this bug report helps Torch developers catch an edge case in the new Metal backend and improve support for MPS!
>
> ⚠️ The following is a diagnosis and explanation generated by ChatGPT-4o
>
> TorchInductor’s Metal (MPS) backend generates invalid .metal shader code when compiling certain reduction-heavy operations under torch.compile(...). Specifically, it emits code where temporary variables and loop indices (e.g., tmp3, r0\_0) are declared inside a loop but accessed after the loop has ended. This violates C++/Metal scoping rules and leads to a hard compile-time SyntaxError.
>
> This issue occurs in multistage reductions, which are triggered when the reduction axis exceeds the maximum threadgroup size (e.g., dimension size > 1024). The faulty code is emitted in torch/\_inductor/codegen/mps.py by the MetalKernel.codegen\_body() method, which inserts store instructions (self.stores) after the reduction loop, despite the necessary values being defined inside the loop.
>
> As a result, valid high-level PyTorch code fails to compile on MPS devices via TorchInductor, even when eager and CUDA backends work fine.
>
> ✅ Minimal Reproducer
>
> ```
> x = torch.randn(1, 1028, device="mps")
> mask = torch.randint(0, 2, (1, 1028), dtype=torch.bool, device="mps")
>
> def masked_softmax(x, mask):
>     x = x.masked_fill(mask, float('-inf'))
>     return torch.nn.functional.softmax(x, dim=-1)
>
> compiled_fn = torch.compile(masked_softmax)
> compiled_fn(x, mask)  # triggers compile error on Metal
> ```
>

> ## [issue:pytorch/pytorch#197805] (issue) [MPS] Process crashes (SIGSEGV/SIGABRT inside Metal) when two Python threads run tensor ops concurrently#197805
> https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/197805
> # \[MPS\] Process crashes (SIGSEGV/SIGABRT inside Metal) when two Python threads run tensor ops concurrently#197805
>
> ## Description
>
> ### 🐛 Describe the bug
>
> Running MPS tensor ops from two Python threads at the same time kills the process; there is no Python exception. The same ops on one thread never crash.
>
> Reproducer (only `torch`, no model; this is the `threads_arange` case of the attached `repro.py`):
>
> ```
> import threading, torch
>
> DTYPES = [torch.float32, torch.float16, torch.bfloat16]
>
> def worker(iters=60):
>     for i in range(iters):
>         dt = DTYPES[i % len(DTYPES)]
>         a = torch.arange(0, 4096 + i, 1, device="mps", dtype=dt)
>         b = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 2048 + i, device="mps", dtype=dt)
>         float(a.float().sum() + b.float().sum())
>

> ## [doc:https://github.com/huggingface/blog/blob/170d160858f63449724c922565ee519a2e333fd8/mps-pytorch-2-15.md] (doc) MPS in PyTorch 2.15
> # MPS in PyTorch 2.15
> ## Getting started
>
> ## Faster language-model decoding
> ### Mixture-of-experts layers
> In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.
>
> For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:
>
> ## [pull_request:pytorch/pytorch#191098] (pull_request) Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.16.0) (oldest at bottom):
> https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/191098
> Stack from ghstack (oldest at bottom):
>
> - \[MPS\] Faster reductions (5/5): migrate min/max from MPSGraph to Metal #191100
> - \[MPS\] Faster reductions (4/5): argmax/argmin strided, split-K and dim=None paths #191099
> - **->**\[MPS\] Faster reductions (3/5): strided/batched outer, small-dim and narrow kernels #191098
> - \[MPS\] Faster reductions (2/5): inner-dim reductions #191097
> - \[MPS\] Faster reductions (1/5): skip input up-casts and vec4 full reductions #191101
> - \[MPS\] Faster reductions (0/5): fix int64 min/max over partial simdgroups #191104
>
> This PR makes MPS reductions faster. The change applies when the reduced dimension is not the last dimension.
>
> Implementation notes
>
> The dispatcher reads each input as a logical `[outer_size, dim_size, inner_size]` shape.
>
> - `outer_size` is the number of independent `[dim_size, inner_size]` matrices. It combines the dimensions before the reduced dimension.
> - `dim_size` is the size of the reduced dimension. Each output value combines `dim_size` input values.
> - `inner_size` is the column count of each matrix. It combines the dimensions after the reduced dimension.
>
> For `[32, 128, 64].sum(1)`, `outer_size` is 32, `dim_size` is 128, and `inner_size` is 64.
>
> Each of the `outer_size` matrices has `inner_size` columns. The dispatcher divides these columns into blocks of 32. One threadgroup processes one column block from one matrix. The threadgroup reduces `dim_size` values for each column. It produces up to 32 output values.
>
> The outer layout starts `outer_size * ceil(inner_size / 32)` threadgroups. For `outer_size = 32` and `inner_size = 64`, each matrix uses 2 threadgroups. So input `[32, 128, 64]` uses 64 threadgroups. One threadgroup processes columns 0 through 31. The other threadgroup processes columns 32 through 63 and this way 32 times
>
> #### Threadgroup size
>
> - `OUTER_TG_WIDTH = 32` sets the output column count for one threadgroup. The thread `x` coordinate selects one inner column. One threadgroup produces up to 32 values of one row of the `[outer_size, inner_size]` output.
> - `OUTER_TG_HEIGHT = 32` sets the thread count for each column. The thread `y` coordinate selects one of these threads. The 32 threads divide the `dim_size` values between them. Without split-K, each thread reads approximately `ceil(dim_size / 32)` values. The threadgroup then combines the 32 partial results into one output value.
>
> One outer threadgroup has `32 * 32 = 1024` threads. Thread `(x, y)` processes one column of the current block. It reads part `y` of the reduced dimension.
>
> `B_block` is the column count of the current block. `B_block` is not more than 32. One outer threadgroup reduces `[1, dim_size, B_block]` to `[1, B_block]`.
>
> For `dim_size = 128`, each column has 32 threads. Each thread reads 4 values from the reduced dimension. The 32 threads then produce one output value for that column.
>
> #### Narrow layout
>
> The outer layout reserves 32 column positions. When `inner_size = 16`, only 16 positions have output columns. Half of the threads do no work.

> # MPS dispatch blocks often fail to propagate C++ exceptions back to the caller#78503
>
> ## Description
>
> ### 🐛 Describe the bug
>
> MPS backend relies on dispatch queues to synchronize code across multiple threads , which fail to propagate C++ exceptions correctly back to the callee, which often results on program termination with unhandled exception, rather than graceful error returned back to the user.

> ## [readme:tashiscool/fp8-mps-metal] (readme) tashiscool/fp8-mps-metal
> https://github.com/tashiscool/fp8-mps-metal
> # fp8-mps-metal
>
> **Custom FP8 compute kernels for Apple Silicon (MPS) — fixing what PyTorch doesn't support yet.**
>
> If you've tried to run FLUX, SD3.5, or any FP8-quantized model on your Mac and hit cryptic errors like `"does not have support for that dtype"` or `"_scaled_mm not implemented for MPS"` — this is the fix. This repo contains a Metal compute shader that performs FP8 (e4m3fn) dequantization and matrix multiplication directly on the GPU, exposed to PyTorch as a drop-in monkey-patch.
>
> > **Tested on:** M4 Pro (48GB), macOS 26.2, PyTorch 2.10.0, Python 3.12
>
> ## Quick Start
>
> ```bash
> git clone https://github.com/tashiscool/fp8-mps-metal.git
> cd fp8-mps-metal
>
> # Option A: Pure Python (no compilation needed — recommended)
> python -c "
> import torch, sys; sys.path.insert(0, '.')
> import fp8_mps_patch
> fp8_mps_patch.install()
> print('FP8 MPS patch installed — FLUX/SD3.5 models should now work')
> "
>
> # Option B: Build C++ extension (slightly different perf characteristics)
> pip install -e .
> ```
>
> No Xcode required. The Metal shader compiles at runtime via `torch.mps.compile_shader()`.
>
> ## What This Solves
>
> PyTorch's MPS backend (Apple's GPU acceleration) has a hard gap: **FP8 tensors exist but can't compute**. This blocks an entire class of modern AI models.
>
> | What works | What doesn't | Impact |
> |-----------|-------------|--------|
> | Create FP8 tensors | Cast float32 → FP8 on MPS | Can't quantize on-device |
> | Transfer FP8 CPU → MPS | `torch._scaled_mm` on MPS | **FLUX/SD3.5 won't run** |
> | FP16/BF16/INT8 compute | Any FP8 arithmetic on MPS | ComfyUI crashes |

Packed prefill and native RMSNorm are implemented and benchmarked on MPS. Both preserved the generated token IDs in the Qwen cases tested.

| Prompt lengths | Padded TTFT | Bucketed TTFT | Packed TTFT |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 22, 132 · FP32 | 0.383s | 0.328s | **0.234s** |
| 22, 132 · FP16 | 0.314s | 0.250s | **0.192s** |
| 22, 32, 132 · FP32 | 0.573s | 0.450s | **0.273s** |

[Packed prefill](./utils/batch.py) is now automatic for heavily imbalanced initial prompts totaling at most 512 tokens; larger or resumed chunks fall back to bucketing. [RMSNorm](./utils/layers.py) now uses [PyTorch’s native operation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.functional.rms_norm.html). In an alternating full-model A/B test, it improved TTFT from 0.419s to 0.397s and decode from about 23.7 to 24.3 tokens/s.

I also added batched-cache-read labels to [profile_engine.py](./profile_engine.py). **251 tests passed, 1 skipped**; `git diff --check` is clean.

I did **not** implement weight-only quantization or a direct Metal paged-attention kernel. This PyTorch MPS build does not implement integer matmul, and no quantized-matmul backend is installed; a useful version would need a dedicated fused kernel, not a weight conversion that runs every token. The current gather/SDPA decode path remains in place.

Two more cached-decode optimizations are in place. [Single-request attention](./utils/attention.py) now shares KV heads instead of duplicating them, and the [KV cache](./utils/kv_cache.py) returns a view when a request’s physical blocks are consecutive. Fragmented layouts retain the existing read path.

Alternating MPS A/B runs showed a modest gain from each change: roughly 3–6% for shared heads and 3–4% for the contiguous view, with identical sampled tokens. In the final same-dtype FP32 matrix, all four cases matched Hugging Face; custom decode ranged from **1.01× to 1.08×** its throughput. The FP16 single-request rows also matched tokens and measured **1.12×–1.16×**, but used only one timed repeat, so treat those speedups cautiously.

I tested a similar batched-read shortcut and reverted it because its gain was inconsistent. **254 tests passed, 1 skipped**; `git diff --check` is clean.
